units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide which details belong in a scientific model for the question being asked.
units.mechanism: A useful scientific model simplifies a real system by keeping details that affect the question and ignoring details that do not affect it.

mx.cwo: An equation for the time of one orbit is not a model of the solar system; only a small ball-and-stick copy that looks like the real thing is a model.
There is one correct model of the human heart, so the same labelled diagram answers a question about blood flow and a question about heart muscle.
Air resistance is always ignored in physics, so a sheet of paper and a coin released together in the classroom reach the floor at the same instant.
In a model of a cricket ball in flight the bright red colour must be kept because it is the most noticeable thing about the ball, while the ball's mass can be left out.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a scientific word or symbol should be interpreted by its precise scientific meaning rather than its everyday meaning.
units.mechanism: Science uses language carefully: familiar words can have specific scientific meanings, and symbols may follow historical or international conventions rather than convenient abbreviations.

mx.cwo: The weight of the school bag is 5 kg, and it will still weigh 5 kg on the Moon.
The sentence 'the prisoner escaped from his cell' is scientifically wrong, because a cell is the basic unit of life.
The symbol for oxygen cannot be O, because chemical symbols never come from the English name of the element.
CO is the symbol for cobalt, because both letters of cobalt appear in it.
Sodium's symbol is So and potassium's is Po, taking the first two letters of each English name.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an equation is being used as a relationship between quantities, not just as a calculation to perform.
units.mechanism: Mathematics in science is a language for expressing relationships between quantities clearly and testing them carefully.

mx.cwo: In F = ma, taking m = 500 g and a = 2 m/s^2 gives F = 1000 N.
Beauty = kindness x 2 is a scientific equation, because it is written in symbols with an equals sign.
In a = F/m, doubling the mass doubles the acceleration, because m appears in the formula.
v = s/t is the speed relationship and s = vt is a different relationship, about distance, so the two cannot be used on the same problem.
From density = mass / volume it follows that mass = density / volume, so a substance of density 2 g/cm3 filling 5 cm3 has a mass of 0.4 g.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether measurements must use the same units and conversions everywhere for a comparison or calculation to be valid.
units.mechanism: Measurements are useful only when units have agreed meanings; using different units or wrong conversions can make a calculation wrong even if the arithmetic is performed.

mx.cwo: The aircraft needed 22300 kilograms of fuel, so pumping in 22300 litres of fuel meets the requirement exactly.
Adding 2 kilograms of flour to 500 grams of sugar gives 502 kilograms of mixture.
A 2 kilometre walk is shorter than a 900 metre walk, because 2 is a much smaller number than 900.
22300 pounds is close enough to 22300 kilograms for refuelling, since both are around twenty thousand and the estimate only needs the right scale.
To change 5 kilograms into grams, divide by 1000, so 5 kilograms is 0.005 grams.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an idea is a scientific law, a scientific theory, or an unsupported guess.
units.mechanism: In science, laws describe patterns, theories explain why patterns occur using evidence available at the time, and a scientific theory is not an untested guess.

mx.cwo: Newton's law of gravitation has been proved, so no new evidence could ever change it.
'Hot air rises' is a scientific law, because it is a short general statement that is always said in science class.
Newton's law of gravitation is a theory because it explains why things fall, and the kinetic theory of gases is a law because gases always behave that way.
Because scientific ideas can always change, the claim that the Earth is flat could still turn out to be right.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a prediction is scientific because it uses measurable evidence and reasoning rather than guesswork.
units.mechanism: A scientific prediction is strengthened when it is based on evidence, reasoning, measurable information, and past patterns.

mx.cwo: The prediction of rain is scientific because the television weather presenter is an expert and said it would rain.
It will rain today because the temperature is 31 degrees Celsius; that is a measurement, so the prediction is scientific.
It did rain that evening, so Varsha's guess from the dark clouds was a scientific prediction after all.
A prediction about which team will win tomorrow can never be scientific, because science only predicts what happens inside a laboratory.
Saying there is a 70 percent chance of rain is scientific, while saying rain is likely because the pressure has fallen sharply is not, since only the first one has a number in it.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a failed prediction shows a limit to the model or theory rather than a reason to reject science by opinion.
units.mechanism: Scientific predictions can fail when conditions are complex, new, or measured more precisely; mismatches with observation are used as evidence to improve ideas.

mx.cwo: The forecast was wrong because the weather scientist made a mistake in the calculation, not because the model has limits.
Newton's laws predicted the planets correctly for centuries, so they must predict the bending of light near the Sun equally well.
The thermometer must have been read wrongly, because the model said the temperature would reach 35 degrees.
Since weather forecasts often fail, an eclipse predicted for a date years ahead is just as likely to be wrong.
The forecast said 30 millimetres of rain and 28 millimetres fell, so the model failed and should be rejected.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to test a popular claim by asking scientific questions about evidence, mechanism, and observable consequences.
units.mechanism: A claim should be checked by asking whether a known mechanism and observable evidence support it, not by accepting it because it is widely circulated.

mx.cwo: Food could possibly become harmful during an eclipse, and since nobody can prove it does not, the warning is supported.
Several people who ate during the eclipse fell ill that night, so eating during an eclipse does spoil food.
Nobody has explained to me how the Moon causes the tides, so that is just a popular belief like the eclipse warning.
An eclipse is a rare and dramatic event, so it must have powerful effects on the body and on food.
Science keeps changing its mind, so the eclipse food warning may turn out to be right and should be followed until it is disproved.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide when a rough estimate is reasonable by choosing assumptions, combining quantities, and checking the scale of the answer.
units.mechanism: A rough estimate can be useful when the aim is a reasonable scale rather than an exact value, as long as the assumptions and quantities are checked for reasonableness.

mx.cwo: A person needs exactly 8640 litres of air a day, so a cylinder holding 8640 litres will last exactly one day.
About 22000 kilograms of fuel is good enough for the flight, since an estimate only needs to have the right scale.
8640 litres per day is a better estimate than about 9000 litres per day, because it has more digits and looks more accurate.
At 15 breaths per minute the daily total is 15 times 24, which is 360 breaths, so a person breathes about 180 litres of air a day.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a real-life problem needs ideas from several branches of science rather than only one branch.
units.mechanism: Many real problems are understood by combining ideas from physics, chemistry, biology, earth science, or other areas instead of treating science as isolated branches.

mx.cwo: A traffic jam has nothing to do with chemistry, because chemistry is about test tubes and there are no test tubes on the road.
Boiling water for tea needs physics, chemistry, biology, earth science and astronomy together, because every real problem needs all the branches.
The question mentions a plant, so it is a biology question and no chemistry or physics is involved in it.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether science should be understood as a human process of curiosity, questioning, collaboration, and testing rather than as a list of facts.
units.mechanism: Science is a human activity shaped by curiosity, creativity, collaboration, careful questioning, observation, testing, and the organisation of ideas.

mx.cwo: Scientists work alone and keep their results secret until they are certain, and only then is the result science.
You cannot ask a scientific question until you have learnt all the facts about the topic, so questions come at the end of science and not at the start.
Watching birds in a park and recording what they eat is not science, because there is no laboratory or apparatus involved.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When describing or judging an object's motion, first choose the reference point and direction needed to state its position at each instant.
units.mechanism: Position is described by the object's distance and direction from a fixed reference point at an instant; motion is identified by change in that position with time.

mx.cwo: The car was at position +30 m during the interval from 2 s to 5 s.
A passenger sitting in a moving train is at rest, and it is simply wrong to say she is moving.
A point 40 m to the left of the origin O has position +40 m, and a point 40 m to the right of O has position -40 m.
The origin is always where the object starts, so a ball thrown from a window has position 0 m at the window whatever origin the question sets.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a question asks for total path length or net change in position before choosing distance travelled or displacement.
units.mechanism: Distance travelled is the total length of path covered and needs only a numerical value with units, while displacement is the net change in position between two instants and needs magnitude and direction.

mx.cwo: A car starts at the 20 km milestone and ends at the 50 km milestone, so its displacement is 50 km.
The distance travelled by the bus is 120 km towards the north.
A boy walks 5 m east and then 3 m back west, so his distance travelled is 2 m and his displacement is 8 m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When finding how fast motion was over a time interval, choose average speed for path length per time and average velocity for displacement per time.
units.mechanism: Average speed = total distance travelled / time interval; average velocity = displacement / time interval and has the direction of displacement.

mx.cwo: The car's average speed for the journey is 60 km/h, because the speedometer read 60 km/h.
The trip was at 40 km/h for the first part and 60 km/h for the second, so the average speed is (40 + 60)/2 = 50 km/h.
For one lap of a 400 m track in 100 s the average speed is 0 m/s and the average velocity is 4 m/s.
Average speed = 100 s / 400 m = 0.25 s/m for one lap of the track.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide acceleration from how velocity changes, including the sign and direction of the change, rather than from speed alone.
units.mechanism: Average acceleration = change in velocity / time interval = (final velocity - initial velocity) / time interval; acceleration has magnitude and direction.

mx.cwo: The car was going at 8 m/s and reaches 20 m/s after 4 s, so its acceleration is 20/4 = 5 m/s^2.
The car reaches 20 m/s from rest in 8 s of stop-start traffic, so its acceleration was 2.5 m/s^2 at every instant of those 8 seconds.
A car slowing from 20 m/s to 5 m/s in 3 s has an acceleration of 5 m/s^2 forwards, in the direction it is travelling.
The lorry has an acceleration because its engine is roaring loudly, even though the speedometer stays at 50 km/h.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Interpret a position-time graph by reading positions and using slope, not by treating the graph as a map of the route.
units.mechanism: A position-time graph shows position on the y-axis against time on the x-axis; the slope between two points gives average velocity over that time interval.

mx.cwo: At t = 4 s the position-time graph is at 20 m, so the velocity at that moment is 20 m/s.
The position-time graph starts at 20 m, so the object had already travelled 20 m before the clock was started.
The area under the position-time graph between 0 s and 4 s is 40, so the displacement in that interval is 40 m.
The slope is 4 s divided by 20 m, so the velocity is 0.2 s/m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Interpret a velocity-time graph's slope to decide whether acceleration is zero, positive, or opposite to velocity.
units.mechanism: On a velocity-time graph, slope equals change in velocity divided by change in time, so it gives acceleration.

mx.cwo: Between 10 s and 20 s the velocity goes from 5 m/s to 10 m/s, so the acceleration is 5 m/s^2.
The line passes through the point (20 s, 10 m/s), so the acceleration is 10 divided by 20, that is 0.5 m/s^2.
Graph B shows the bigger acceleration because its line is at a steeper angle on the paper, even though its velocity axis is marked in steps of 1 m/s and graph A's in steps of 10 m/s.
Between 0 s and 10 s the line sits at 5 m/s, so the acceleration is 5 x 10 = 50 m/s^2.
The acceleration is 10 s divided by 5 m/s, giving 2 s^2/m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use the area between a velocity-time graph and the time axis to find displacement over a selected interval.
units.mechanism: For a velocity-time graph, the area enclosed by the graph line and the time axis over a time interval equals displacement in that interval.

mx.cwo: The displacement between 0 s and 10 s is 0.5, because the slope of the velocity-time line is 0.5 m/s^2.
The areas are +50 m above the axis and -20 m below it, so the total distance travelled is 30 m.
The line rises from 0 to 20 m/s over 8 s, so the displacement is 20 x 8 = 160 m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Choose and apply the constant-acceleration kinematic equation that matches the known and unknown quantities.
units.mechanism: For straight-line motion with constant acceleration, v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at^2, and v^2 = u^2 + 2as relate displacement, time interval, initial velocity, final velocity, and acceleration.

mx.cwo: With u = 20 m/s, a = -5 m/s^2 and s = 40 m, v = u + at gives v = 20 - 5 x 40 = -180 m/s.
A cyclist covers 500 m in 40 s in stop-start city traffic, so s = ut + half a t squared with u = 0 gives a = 0.625 m/s^2.
A ball thrown up at 20 m/s returns to the hand after 4 s, and s = ut + half a t squared gives s = 0, so the ball travelled no distance at all.
For a car braking from 25 m/s to rest over 60 m, using u squared = v squared + 2as gives 625 = 0 + 120a, so a = +5.2 m/s^2.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a motion can be modelled as one-dimensional straight-line motion, motion in a plane, or motion in space before choosing the representation.
units.mechanism: Linear motion is motion in a straight line; motion in a plane is two-dimensional; motion in space is three-dimensional.

mx.cwo: A ball rolling along a straight groove is three-dimensional motion, because the ball is a three-dimensional object moving in three-dimensional space.
A ball thrown straight up and caught again is two-dimensional motion, because it goes up and then comes back down.
A ball thrown at an angle covers 45 m along its curved path, from s = ut + half a t squared with u = 15 m/s and t = 3 s.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For circular motion over a full revolution, separate distance and average speed from displacement and average velocity.
units.mechanism: In one revolution on a circular path of radius R, distance travelled is the circumference 2piR, average speed is 2piR/T, displacement is 0, and average velocity over that time interval is 0.

mx.cwo: For one revolution of a circle of radius 7 m the distance travelled is 14 m.
After a quarter of a lap of the circular track the runner's displacement is zero, because displacement is always zero on a circle.
The average speed for one lap of a radius 7 m circle in 20 s is 2 x pi x 49 / 20 = 15.4 m/s.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Recognise that uniform circular motion is accelerated even when speed is constant, because the direction of velocity changes.
units.mechanism: Uniform circular motion means motion in a circular path with constant speed; the speed stays constant at every point, but velocity direction changes, so acceleration is nonzero.

mx.cwo: At the top of the circle the whirling stone's velocity points towards the centre of the circle.
A stone whirled faster and faster on a string is in uniform circular motion, because its path is a circle.
A satellite in a nearly circular orbit is not really in uniform circular motion, so it has no acceleration.
The stone on the string is not accelerating, because it stays the same distance from my hand the whole time.
Over one full revolution the average velocity is zero, so the acceleration in uniform circular motion is zero.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a force description is complete only when both its magnitude and direction are known.
units.mechanism: A force can make an object start moving, stop, change speed, change direction, or change shape, and its effect changes if either the magnitude or the direction changes.

mx.cwo: The spring balance shows that the boy pulled the block with a force of 2 kg.
Gravity does not need a direction stated, because it is not a push or a pull that anybody applies.
The 3 N force is bigger than the 8 N force, because its arrow is drawn longer in the diagram.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether the forces on one object are balanced or unbalanced by using the net force.
units.mechanism: When several forces act on the same object, the object's motion depends on the net force; balanced forces give zero net force, while unbalanced forces give a non-zero net force.

mx.cwo: The forces on the 2 kg block are balanced, because the 20 N upward push from the table is much bigger than its 2 kg mass.
The horse pulls the cart with 200 N and the cart pulls back on the horse with 200 N, so the net force is zero and the cart cannot move.
The forces on a parachutist falling at a steady 5 m/s are unbalanced, because he is clearly moving downwards.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Calculate the magnitude and direction of the net force when collinear forces act on one object.
units.mechanism: For forces in the same direction, add their magnitudes; for opposite unequal forces, subtract the smaller from the larger and take the direction of the larger force.

mx.cwo: Forces of 10 N and 6 N act in the same direction on the box, so the net force is 8 N in that direction.
A 3 N force acts north and a 4 N force acts east, so the net force on the object is 7 N.
A 10 N force acts to the right and a 6 N force to the left, so the net force is 4 N to the left.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Predict whether friction will keep a pushed object at rest, let it start moving, or bring a moving object to rest.
units.mechanism: Friction acts between surfaces in contact and opposes the applied push or the direction of motion; an object starts moving only when the applied force is larger than the opposing friction, and a moving object slows if friction is not countered.

mx.cwo: The heavier box needs a bigger push to start moving because its weight pushes backwards against the push.
Pushing a stationary crate with 20 N against 20 N of friction sets the crate moving, because the push has matched the friction.
Opening a parachute makes no difference to how fast a skydiver falls, because air friction can be neglected.
A brick lying on its large face needs a bigger push to start sliding than the same brick standing on its small end, because more of it is touching the floor.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Compare surfaces by inferring the relative friction from distance travelled or spring-balance reading.
units.mechanism: The force of friction depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact; for the same launch, smaller friction lets the object travel farther, and a smaller spring-balance reading indicates smaller friction.

mx.cwo: Glass has a friction of 2 N, because friction is a property of the glass itself.
Surface A has less friction than surface B, because the block ran 60 cm on A after a hard flick and only 30 cm on B after a gentle flick.
The tiled floor must have less friction than the wooden floor because it looks shinier, so the spring-balance readings are not needed.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use Newton's first law to decide what happens when the net force on an object is zero.
units.mechanism: If the net force on an object is zero, an object at rest remains at rest and a moving object continues with constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero.

mx.cwo: The book resting on the table has no forces acting on it at all, which is why it stays still.
A car going round a bend at a steady 50 km/h has zero net force on it, because its velocity is constant.
A hockey puck sliding across smooth ice has a forward force on it that is being used up as it goes.
The net force on the sliding box is zero, so the friction on it must be zero too and the floor is frictionless.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use Newton's second law to determine acceleration or force from net force and mass.
units.mechanism: When a net force acts on an object, the object accelerates in the direction of the net force; acceleration is directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass, so a = F/m and F = ma.

mx.cwo: A 10 N pull on a 2 kg trolley that also experiences 4 N of friction gives an acceleration of 5 m/s^2.
A 500 g trolley accelerated at 2 m/s^2 needs a force of 1000 N.
The 2 kg toy car and the 2 kg brick both get a 4 N push, but the brick accelerates less because it looks heavier and more solid.
A 3 kg trolley is pulled horizontally with 6 N, so its acceleration is 9.8 m/s^2, since F = mg gives the force on it.
A net force of 12 N on a 4 kg box gives an acceleration of 4 divided by 12, that is 0.33 m/s^2.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Calculate gravitational force near Earth's surface and the balancing support force for a steady object.
units.mechanism: Near Earth's surface, gravitational force on an object is F = mg with g about 9.8 m s^-2, and a steady supported object needs an equal upward force to balance its weight.

mx.cwo: The barbell is being held still, so its acceleration is 0 and F = mg gives a gravitational force of 0 N on it.
An astronaut of mass 70 kg on the Moon has a weight of 686 N, because F = mg with g = 9.8 m/s^2.
A lift accelerating upwards at 2 m/s^2 still pushes up on a 60 kg passenger with exactly 588 N, because the support force always equals the weight.
The gravitational force on a 30 kg barbell is 30 divided by 9.8, that is 3.06 N.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Explain why increasing stopping time reduces the force during catching, cushioning, or collision.
units.mechanism: For a moving object that must be brought to rest, increasing the time over which its motion changes makes the required stopping force smaller, while stopping it abruptly requires a larger force.

mx.cwo: The airbag reduces the force on the car, which is why the crash is less severe.
A cricket ball caught slowly needs less force than a tennis ball caught quickly, so catching slowly is what makes the difference.
Pushing a stalled car for a longer time means you need less force to get it moving.
A thin foam mat protects a falling gymnast just as well as a thick one, because both mats are soft.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use motion graphs to decide whether a net force acts and, when possible, calculate the force.
units.mechanism: A net force acts when velocity changes; on a velocity-time graph the slope gives acceleration, and multiplying that acceleration by mass gives force.

mx.cwo: The position-time graph has slope 4 m/s, so the net force on the 2 kg object is 8 N.
The velocity-time line has slope 3 m/s^2, so the net force on the object is 3 N.
The 5 kg object's velocity-time line rises steadily, so the net force on it is 5 x 9.8 = 49 N.
The line runs from (0 s, 0 m/s) to (5 s, 20 m/s), so the acceleration is 5/20 = 0.25 m/s^2 and the force on the 3 kg object is 0.75 N.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Identify the Newton's third law pair in an interaction without treating the pair as balanced forces on one object.
units.mechanism: Whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force on the first object; the two forces act on different objects.

mx.cwo: The action and reaction forces on the book are its 5 N weight downwards and the 5 N push of the table upwards.
The horse and cart cannot move, because the horse's 500 N pull on the cart is cancelled by the cart's 500 N pull on the horse.
Newton's third law does not apply to gravity, because the Earth and the apple never touch each other.
The lorry exerts a larger force on the car in the crash, because the lorry is much bigger and it was the one doing the hitting.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Explain forward motion in walking, paddling, and rockets by identifying the reaction force on the moving object.
units.mechanism: A person, canoe, balloon, or rocket moves because it pushes another object or expelled material in one direction and receives an equal opposite force in the other direction.

mx.cwo: A rocket moves forward because its exhaust pushes against the air behind it, which is why a rocket cannot work in space.
A person can walk normally on a perfectly frictionless floor, because they still push backwards on it.
Firing the rocket's engine forwards while it is already moving forwards makes it go faster, because engines always add speed.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether equal and opposite interaction forces must produce equal accelerations.
units.mechanism: Equal and opposite forces on two interacting objects do not generally produce equal accelerations, because each acceleration also depends on the mass of the object receiving the force.

mx.cwo: The 0.1 kg bullet weighs 0.98 N, so the 2 N force gives it an acceleration of 2 divided by 0.98, that is 2.04 m/s^2.
The 5 kg gun recoils with a larger acceleration than the 0.1 kg bullet, because the gun has more mass for the same 2 N force to work with.
The Earth does not accelerate at all when an apple falls, because nothing about the Earth moves.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Treat connected objects as one system when calculating their acceleration from an external force.
units.mechanism: For connected objects considered as one system on a frictionless horizontal surface, the system accelerates like a single object whose mass is the total mass, so a = F/(m1 + m2).

mx.cwo: The system is pulled with 15 N and the string tension is 9 N, so the total force on the 5 kg system is 24 N and the acceleration is 4.8 m/s^2.
Two connected boxes on a rough floor still accelerate at the applied force divided by the total mass, because that is the system formula.
The tension in the string between the two boxes is 15 N, the same as the applied force, because the system behaves like one object.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether scientific work is being done by a specified force on a specified object.
units.mechanism: Work is done by a force on an object only when that force brings about displacement of the object in the direction of the force; for a constant force, work equals force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force.

mx.cwo: force still holds here even though The force or agency doing the work and the object on which the work is done must be is missing from the stem.
Agency is what produces force, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The force rule also covers this: The same definition applies for vertical, horizontal, or any other direction when the displacement is in the, so it is not an exception.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Determine whether the work done by a force is positive, negative, or zero from the relative directions of force and displacement.
units.mechanism: Work has no direction, but it can be positive, negative, or zero: work is positive when displacement is in the direction of the force, negative when displacement is opposite to the force, and zero when there is no displacement in the force's direction.

mx.cwo: positive work still holds here even though The force doing work and the object on which it acts must be identified before assigning is missing from the stem.
The positive work rule also covers this: Equal and opposite interaction forces can do work with different signs on different objects, so it is not an exception.

The answer is positive work because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Determine whether the work done by a force is positive, negative, or' as the operative test.
positive work is settled by running 'Identify potential energy stored by deformation or relative position': Potential energy is energy stored by deformation of an object or by the relative positions.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Calculate work from force and displacement, including by using the area under a force-displacement graph.
units.mechanism: For a constant force in the direction of displacement, W = F * s; on a force-displacement graph, work equals the area under the graph between the initial and final positions, including when the force is not constant.

mx.cwo: work still holds here even though The displacement axis must represent displacement in the direction of the force is missing from the stem.
Constant force is what produces work, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The work rule also covers this: Work is measured in joules, with 1 J equal to 1 N m, so it is not an exception.
work is settled by running 'Decide what a fixed pulley or a movable pulley changes in a lifting': A fixed pulley can change the direction of effort so that pulling downward raises the load.
Work is found by dividing the given values instead of multiplying, giving 83 as the reported result.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use the work-energy theorem to connect work done on an object or system to its change in energy.
units.mechanism: Work done on an object appears as a change in its energy; positive work increases the object's energy and negative work decreases it.

mx.cwo: Work is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Use the work-energy theorem to connect work done on an object or' is answered as work rather than work-energy theorem.
work-energy theorem still holds here even though The object or system whose energy is changing must be identified is missing from the stem.
Work is what produces work-energy theorem, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The work-energy theorem rule also covers this: Energy and work are both measured in joules, so it is not an exception.

The answer is work-energy theorem because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Use the work-energy theorem to connect work done on an object or' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Identify the form of energy present and the energy transformation taking place in a situation.
units.mechanism: Energy is the capacity to do work, can exist in many forms, and can be converted from one form to another; mechanical energy is energy due to an object's motion or position.

Electric current is found by multiplying the given values instead of dividing, giving 14 as the reported result.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how potential difference, work, charge, and energy per coulomb are related.
units.mechanism: Potential difference between two points is the work done to move unit charge between them: V = W/Q, so W = VQ; 1 V = 1 J/C.

mx.cwo: potential difference still holds here even though The relationship applies between two points of an electric circuit carrying current is missing from the stem.
Work is what produces potential difference, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The potential difference rule also covers this: The statement '1 V' means 1 joule of work is done per coulomb of charge, so it is not an exception.
potential difference is settled by running 'Decide how to replace a parallel combination of resistors by one': In a parallel combination, the total current is the sum of branch currents and 1/R_p =.
Potential difference is found by multiplying the given values instead of dividing, giving 43 as the reported result.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide where to place an ammeter or voltmeter when measuring a circuit quantity.
units.mechanism: An ammeter measures current and is connected in series through the path whose current is measured; a voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel across the two points being compared.

mx.cwo: Voltmeter is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide where to place an ammeter or voltmeter when measuring a circuit' is answered as voltmeter rather than ammeter.
Voltmeter is what produces ammeter, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.

The answer is ammeter because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Decide where to place an ammeter or voltmeter when measuring a circuit' as the operative test.
ammeter is settled by running 'Decide how potential difference, work, charge, and energy per coulomb': Potential difference between two points is the work done to move unit charge between them.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide from a circuit diagram whether components form a series path, parallel branches, or a mixed combination.
units.mechanism: Resistors joined end to end are in series; resistors connected between the same two points are in parallel; a mixed circuit contains both kinds of connection.

mx.cwo: Resistor is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide from a circuit diagram whether components form a series path' is answered as resistor rather than circuit diagram.
circuit diagram still holds here even though Classify the connection by tracing paths and endpoints, not by the physical spacing of is missing from the stem.
The circuit diagram rule also covers this: A parallel group has separate branches connected between the same two points, so it is not an exception.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide when Ohm's law can be used to relate voltage, current, and resistance.
units.mechanism: For a given metallic wire at a given temperature, V/I is constant and equals resistance R; therefore V = IR, R = V/I, and I = V/R.

mx.cwo: Potential difference is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide when Ohm's law can be used to relate voltage, current, and' is answered as potential difference rather than Ohm's law.
Potential difference is what produces Ohm's law, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
Ohm's law is settled by running 'Decide how potential difference, work, charge, and energy per coulomb': Potential difference between two points is the work done to move unit charge between them.
Ohm's law is found by multiplying the given values instead of dividing, giving 49 as the reported result.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how changing a conductor's length, cross-sectional area, or material changes its resistance.
units.mechanism: For a conductor, R is directly proportional to length, inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, and equals rho l/A, where rho is the material's resistivity.

mx.cwo: Length is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide how changing a conductor's length, cross-sectional area, or' is answered as length rather than resistance.
resistance still holds here even though Compare length or area effects while keeping the material the same is missing from the stem.
Length is what produces resistance, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The resistance rule also covers this: Resistivity is a characteristic property of the material and has SI unit ohm m, so it is not an exception.

The answer is resistance because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Decide how changing a conductor's length, cross-sectional area, or' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a material is better treated as a conductor, insulator, or heating-element material from its resistivity and high-temperature behaviour.
units.mechanism: Metals have very low resistivity and are good conductors; insulators have very high resistivity; alloys generally have higher resistivity than their constituent metals and do not oxidise readily at high temperatures, so they are commonly used in electrical heating devices.

mx.cwo: metal still holds here even though Use the tabulated resistivity values when comparing named materials at 20 degrees Celsius is missing from the stem.
The metal rule also covers this: A thick wire of the same material and length has lower resistance than a thin wire, so geometry still matters, so it is not an exception.

The answer is metal because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Decide whether a material is better treated as a conductor, insulator' as the operative test.
metal is settled by running 'Decide when Ohm's law can be used to relate voltage, current, and': For a given metallic wire at a given temperature, V/I is constant and equals resistance R.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to replace a series combination of resistors by one equivalent resistance.
units.mechanism: In a series combination, the same current flows through every resistor, total potential difference equals the sum of the individual potential differences, and equivalent resistance is R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + ... .

mx.cwo: Same current is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide how to replace a series combination of resistors by one' is answered as same current rather than series resistors.
series resistors still holds here even though Apply this rule only to resistors joined end to end in a single path is missing from the stem.

The answer is series resistors because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Decide how to replace a series combination of resistors by one' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to replace a parallel combination of resistors by one equivalent resistance.
units.mechanism: In a parallel combination, the total current is the sum of branch currents and 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3 + ... .

mx.cwo: Branch current is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide how to replace a parallel combination of resistors by one' is answered as branch current rather than parallel resistors.
Branch current is what produces parallel resistors, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.

parallel resistors is settled by running 'Decide how potential difference, work, charge, and energy per coulomb': Potential difference between two points is the work done to move unit charge between them.
Parallel resistors is found by multiplying the given values instead of dividing, giving 33 as the reported result.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to solve a circuit that combines series and parallel resistor groups.
units.mechanism: A mixed resistor circuit is simplified by replacing each identifiable series or parallel group with its equivalent resistance, then using the resulting total resistance with Ohm's law.

mx.cwo: Series group is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide how to solve a circuit that combines series and parallel' is answered as series group rather than mixed circuit.
mixed circuit still holds here even though First identify which resistors share the same two endpoints and which lie end to end in a is missing from the stem.
Series group is what produces mixed circuit, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The mixed circuit rule also covers this: Use the battery potential difference and final equivalent resistance to calculate total current, so it is not an exception.

The answer is mixed circuit because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Decide how to solve a circuit that combines series and parallel' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a practical device should be connected in series or in parallel with other devices.
units.mechanism: A series circuit carries the same current throughout, so devices needing different operating currents are impractical in series; parallel branches allow separate branch currents while sharing the supply potential difference.

mx.cwo: Parallel circuit is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide whether a practical device should be connected in series or in' is answered as parallel circuit rather than series circuit.
Parallel circuit is what produces series circuit, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.

series circuit is settled by running 'Decide how potential difference, work, charge, and energy per coulomb': Potential difference between two points is the work done to move unit charge between them.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how much heat is produced by an electric current and what that implies for heating elements, filaments, and fuses.
units.mechanism: Electrical energy supplied to a resistor is dissipated as heat; for a steady current, Joule's law gives H = I^2Rt, so heat is proportional to the square of current, to resistance, and to time.

mx.cwo: Joule's law of heating still holds here even though Apply H = I^2Rt to a resistor carrying steady current is missing from the stem.
The Joule's law of heating rule also covers this: A fuse is placed in series and stops the circuit when unduly high current produces enough heating, so it is not an exception.

The answer is Joule's law of heating because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Decide how much heat is produced by an electric current and what that' as the operative test.

Joule's law of heating is settled by running 'Decide how to replace a parallel combination of resistors by one': In a parallel combination, the total current is the sum of branch currents and 1/R_p =.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to calculate electric power, electrical energy used, and commercial energy cost.
units.mechanism: Electric power is the rate of electrical energy consumption: P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R, and electrical energy equals power multiplied by time; 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

mx.cwo: electric power still holds here even though Use watt for power; 1 W is the power used when 1 A flows at 1 V is missing from the stem.
Cost. is what produces At fixed voltage and current, power increases with their product; for a device of fixed power, longer, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The electric power rule also covers this: Use P = VI when voltage and current are known, and use I^2R or V^2/R when resistance is part of the known, so it is not an exception.
Electric power is found by dividing the given values instead of multiplying, giving 70 as the reported result.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic effect, visible as compass-needle deflection near the conductor.
units.mechanism: An electric current through a metallic conductor produces a magnetic field around it, so a nearby compass needle can be deflected.

mx.cwo: With the switch open the compass beside the wire still deflects, because the cell has already put charge onto the copper.
A compass 5 m away from the wire deflects by the same amount as one placed 1 cm from it, since the same current is flowing.
Holding a bar magnet next to a copper wire that is joined to nothing makes a current flow in the wire, so the bulb in the loop lights up.
A straight current-carrying wire cannot deflect the compass; the wire has to be wound into a coil first so that it looks like a magnet.
On closing the switch the copper wire swings sideways while the compass needle stays pointing north.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Interpret magnetic field lines as a representation of magnetic field direction, relative strength, and the impossibility of two directions at one point.
units.mechanism: Magnetic field has both direction and magnitude; the field direction is the direction in which a north pole of a compass needle moves, closer field lines show stronger field, and field lines do not cross.

mx.cwo: Outside the bar magnet the field lines are drawn from the south pole to the north pole, because the needle's south end points that way.
Between two bar magnets placed side by side the field lines are allowed to cross, because each magnet has its own set of lines.
The field is strongest far from the bar magnet where the lines are spread out, and weakest near the poles where they are bunched together.
Iron filings move along the field lines from the north pole to the south pole, and the space between two lines has no magnetic field at all.
The diagram with 12 field lines drawn shows a stronger field everywhere than the diagram with 8, even where the 8 lines are packed much closer together.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Predict the pattern and strength change of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying conductor.
units.mechanism: The magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor forms concentric circles around the wire; compass deflection changes when the current changes and becomes smaller when the compass is moved farther from the conductor.

mx.cwo: The field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are straight lines pointing outward from the wire like the spokes of a wheel.
The circles lie in the same plane as the wire, so a compass placed directly along the wire's own line shows the strongest circular deflection.
Moving the compass from 1 cm to 5 cm away from the wire makes the needle swing further, because the field lines have spread out to reach it.
A 10 cm piece of wire carrying 2 A is too short to have a magnetic field around it, so a compass beside it will not deflect.
The thick copper wire gives a bigger compass deflection than the thin one, even though both carry 2 A and the compass is 2 cm from each.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use the right-hand thumb rule to determine the direction of magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor.
units.mechanism: If a straight current-carrying conductor is held in the right hand with the thumb pointing in the direction of current, the curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field around the conductor.

mx.cwo: With the current flowing upward in the wire, the field circles clockwise when seen from above, because the curled left-hand fingers go that way.
Electrons drift from the negative terminal upward through the wire, so the thumb points up and the field circles anticlockwise seen from above.
The right-hand thumb rule cannot be used for a wire lying flat on the bench, because the thumb has to point up or down.
With current flowing north in the wire, the magnetic field points straight into the page, because that is where the thumb ends up.
For a wire carrying current to the north, the magnetic field points north along the wire and the current circles around it.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Transfer the current-field rule from a straight wire to a circular loop or coil, including the effect of multiple turns.
units.mechanism: A current-carrying circular loop produces magnetic field lines determined by the direction of current, and a circular coil with n turns produces n times the magnetic field of a single turn at a given point when the same current passes through each turn.

mx.cwo: Two coils made from the same 2 m of wire give the same field at their centres, whether it is wound as 4 turns or as 20 turns.
Winding 10 turns side by side across the same cell gives 10 times the field of one turn, whatever the current in each turn turns out to be.
A 10-turn coil gives one tenth of the field of a single turn at its centre, because the magnetism is shared out among the ten turns.
Adding turns multiplies the field by 10 at every point around the coil, so the pattern of the field lines is exactly the same shape ten times over.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Recognise how a current-carrying solenoid behaves magnetically and how it can make an electromagnet.
units.mechanism: A solenoid is a coil of many closely wound circular turns of insulated copper wire in the shape of a cylinder; when current flows, its magnetic field pattern is like that of a bar magnet, and a strong field inside it can magnetise soft iron to form an electromagnet.

mx.cwo: A solenoid wound on a copper rod makes just as strong an electromagnet as one wound on a soft-iron rod.
The field just outside the solenoid is the same everywhere too, so a compass 1 cm from the coil reads the same as one 20 cm away.
Inside the solenoid the field is strongest at the two ends, where the turns look crowded together in the drawing, and weakest halfway along.
A current-carrying solenoid has no north or south end; its field lines are simply circles around each individual turn of wire.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide when a current-carrying conductor experiences a force in a magnetic field and how reversing current or field changes that force direction.
units.mechanism: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force; the direction of the force depends on the direction of current and the direction of the magnetic field, and the force is perpendicular to both when current and field are perpendicular.

mx.cwo: With the rod turned so the current runs from the north pole to the south pole, along the field, it is still pushed sideways with the same force as before.
A wire lying on the bench with 3 A flowing through it is pushed sideways by its own magnetic field, with no magnet needed.
The rod always moves toward the north pole of the magnet, because that is the stronger end of the field.
On closing the switch the two magnets swing apart while the aluminium rod stays where it is, because the rod's own field pushes on them.
With the field pointing from north to south across the rod, the rod is pushed along that same north-to-south direction.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule to determine the force direction on a current-carrying conductor or moving charged particle in a magnetic field.
units.mechanism: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the forefinger shows magnetic field, the middle finger shows current, and the thumb shows force; for an electron, conventional current is opposite to the electron's motion.

mx.cwo: With the field pointing right and the current upward, the force on the conductor comes out of the page.
Fleming's left-hand rule cannot be used for an electron moving through a magnetic field, because there is no wire and so no current to put on the middle finger.
With the current upward, the force on the conductor curls around the wire in the anticlockwise sense given by the curled fingers.
Field to the right on the forefinger and current upward on the middle finger gives the force into the page; with the two swapped the answer is written as out of the page instead.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Classify the roles of live, neutral, and earth wires in a domestic circuit and recognise why appliances are connected across live and neutral in separate circuits.
units.mechanism: Domestic supply uses live, neutral, and earth wires; different appliances are connected across the live and neutral wires in separate circuits, each with a separate switch, and the live-neutral potential difference shown is 220 V.

mx.cwo: The earth wire brings the 220 V supply into the house and the live wire is the safety wire connected to the metal body of the appliance.
The fan, the lamp and the heater are joined one after another along the live wire, so switching off the lamp switches off the fan as well.
A short circuit in the kitchen branch cannot blow the main fuse or affect the lights, because each appliance is on its own separate circuit.
The earth wire melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows, which is why a metal-bodied appliance needs one.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Explain why an electric fuse is placed in domestic circuits as a safety component.
units.mechanism: An electric fuse is an important component of domestic circuits because it prevents damage to appliances and circuits when unsafe current conditions occur.

mx.cwo: A fuse is fitted so that any current leaking to the metal body of an appliance is carried safely into the ground instead of through the user.
A fuse wired into the earth lead beside the appliance protects it just as well as one in the live supply lead.
Replace the 5 A fuse in the lighting circuit with a 30 A one so that the circuit is better protected.
Once the main fuse is fitted at the distribution box, no separate fuse or switch is needed in any branch, since one fuse covers the whole house.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When a physical quantity is measured, decide that the result must pair a numerical value with a suitable unit based on an accepted reference standard.
units.mechanism: A measurement compares a physical quantity with an accepted reference standard called a unit, and the measured result is expressed as a number accompanied by that unit.

mx.cwo: In the measurement 5.0 m, the physical quantity is the metre and the unit is length.
The length of the table is 5 handspans, and that is a complete measurement because a handspan is the unit I chose.
A length of 5.0 m is 0.050 cm, because the centimetre is smaller than the metre so the number must get smaller too.
The refractive index of glass must be written as 1.5 m/m, because a number without a unit is never a complete result.
A count of 12 eggs is a measurement of a physical quantity, since it is a number written with its unit after it.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When a unit appears, decide whether it is an SI base unit, an SI derived unit, or a non-SI unit retained with a stated SI conversion.
units.mechanism: SI uses seven base units, derives other physical units from the base units, and also allows some named non-SI units to be used through stated values in SI units.

mx.cwo: The newton is an SI base unit, and the kilogram is a derived unit obtained from it.
The sample contains 2 mol, and that is a complete statement of the amount of substance without saying what is being counted.
Since the litre and the light year are allowed alongside SI, the mile and the pound are acceptable SI units too.
N is a base unit because it is written as one capital letter, while m s^-1 is derived because its symbol has two parts.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When reading a measured number, decide which digits are significant, especially zeros and powers of ten.
units.mechanism: Significant figures are the reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit; non-zero digits are significant, zeros between non-zero digits are significant, trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant, and powers of ten do not change the significant-figure count.

mx.cwo: The measurement 0.0250 m has four significant figures, because there are four digits after the decimal point.
The measurement 4500 m has four significant figures, since every printed digit belongs to the measurement.
0.002500 has four significant figures: the two zeros in front of the 2 count and the two zeros after the 5 do not.
A diameter measured as 2 cm carries an unlimited number of significant figures, just like the 2 in r = d/2.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When calculating with measured values, decide which rounding rule to apply for multiplication or division versus addition or subtraction.
units.mechanism: For multiplication or division, the final result keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures; for addition or subtraction, the final result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.

mx.cwo: T = 21.4 s divided by 20 oscillations is 1.07 s, which must be reported as 1.1 s because the 20 has only two significant figures.
0.0025 x 4.0 = 0.0, because 4.0 has only one decimal place and the product must be given to one decimal place.
The circumference of a circle of radius 2.4567 m can only be given as 15.4 m, because pi was taken as 3.14 and that has three significant figures.
2.5 x 1.234 = 3.085, kept to four significant figures because 1.234 is the more precise of the two factors.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When reporting a result from measured data, decide how the uncertainties in the measurements limit the quoted value and its error.
units.mechanism: Every measurement has uncertainty, and when measured values are combined, the final reported value must reflect the uncertainty carried by the data and be quoted with an appropriate rounded error.

mx.cwo: The area is 4.7 m^2 with an error of 2 m^2, because the two percentage uncertainties added to 2 per cent.
The area of a sheet 1.5 m by 3.175 m is 4.7625 m^2, because the more precise measurement 3.175 m fixes how precisely the area is known.
The difference between 2.10 m and 2.05 m, each known to 1 per cent, is 0.05 m with a percentage error of 2 per cent.
A mass of 1.02 g and a mass of 9.98 g are both given to three significant figures, so both carry the same relative error of 0.1 per cent.
A mass of 20.0 g measured to within 0.1 g has a percentage error of 200 per cent.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When describing a physical quantity, decide its dimensional formula in terms of base dimensions such as M, L, and T.
units.mechanism: A physical quantity represented by a derived unit can be expressed as a combination of base dimensions; in mechanics, quantities are written using dimensions such as M, L, and T, and magnitudes are not considered.

mx.cwo: The dimensional formula of force is kg m s^-2.
The dimensional formula of kinetic energy is (1/2) M L^2 T^-2.
The dimensional formula of temperature is M^0 L^0 T^0, so temperature is a dimensionless quantity.
For E = m c^2 the dimensional formula is M L^2, because only a mass and a squared length appear in the equation.
The dimensional formula of density is M^-1 L^3, obtained from volume divided by mass.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When checking an equation, decide whether every added or subtracted term has the same dimensions as the other terms and the opposite side.
units.mechanism: Only physical quantities with the same dimensions can be added or subtracted, and an equation is dimensionally consistent when every term on both sides has the same dimensions.

mx.cwo: The sum 3 kg + 2 g is dimensionally inconsistent, because the two terms are not written in the same unit.
The equation x = v t + 5 is dimensionally consistent, because 5 is only a number and a number can be added to anything.
The relation v^2 = v0^2 + 3 a x must be correct, because both sides have the dimensions L^2 T^-2.
In s = u t + (1/2) a t^3 only the left and right sides need to match, and since the right side contains a length term the equation passes the test.
v = u + a t fails the test, because the right-hand side gives L T^-1 + L T^-1 = L^2 T^-2, which does not match L T^-1 on the left.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When deriving a relation by dimensional analysis, decide the product form, equate the powers of base dimensions, and recognize what the method cannot determine.
units.mechanism: If the dependence of a physical quantity on other quantities is known, the quantity can be written as a dimensionless constant times powers of those quantities; equating dimensions gives the exponents, but dimensional analysis cannot determine dimensionless constants.

mx.cwo: Dimensional analysis gives T = sqrt(l/g) exactly, so a 1.0 m pendulum has a period of 0.32 s.
Because the launch angle is dimensionless, dimensional analysis shows that the range of a projectile is v0^2/g at every angle.
Equating the powers gives T = k sqrt(g/l), so a longer pendulum has a shorter period.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Can the moving body be treated as a point object for this motion?
units.mechanism: A body may be treated as a point object when its size is much smaller than the distance it moves during the time being considered.

mx.cwo: A cricket ball can always be treated as a point object because a ball is a small thing, while a train never can.
The 200 m train may be treated as a point object while it moves the first 50 m out of the station, because it travels 500 km during the day.
A 4 m long car reversing 2 m into a parking space can be treated as a point object, because its length is bigger than the distance it moves.
Since the Earth is a point object in its orbit round the Sun, it has no size and therefore cannot spin on its own axis.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Has an origin and positive direction been fixed before assigning signs to position, displacement, velocity, or acceleration?
units.mechanism: In one-dimensional motion, position is specified relative to a chosen origin, and the signs of displacement, velocity, and acceleration follow the chosen positive direction.

mx.cwo: The car starts 30 m to the right of the origin, so its position at t = 0 is x = 0 and after moving 12 m further it is x = 12 m.
With downward chosen as the positive direction, a ball that falls 20 m has a displacement of -20 m and a velocity of -14 m s^-1.
A particle at x = -5 m is closer to the origin than one at x = +2 m, because -5 is a smaller number than 2.
A position of -3 m cannot be right because a distance cannot be less than nothing, so the position is 3 m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Should the interval quantity be calculated from total path length or from net displacement?
units.mechanism: Average velocity is displacement divided by time interval, while average speed is total path length divided by time interval; instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity.

mx.cwo: At t = 3 s the car's instantaneous speed is 12 m s^-1 while the magnitude of its instantaneous velocity is only 9 m s^-1, because the road is curved.
A runner who goes 100 m east in 20 s and comes straight back in 20 s has an average velocity of 5 m s^-1 and an average speed of zero.
Even for a car driven 60 km straight down one road in 1 h, the average speed must be larger than the magnitude of the average velocity.
On a curved road only the average speed can be found; the average velocity needs a straight road, so it does not exist here.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Is velocity at an instant being found from the limiting slope of the position-time graph, not from an arbitrary finite interval average?
units.mechanism: Instantaneous velocity is v = lim(Delta t -> 0) Delta x / Delta t = dx/dt, the slope of the tangent to the position-time graph at that instant.

mx.cwo: Since the average velocity over the whole trip from 0 to 8.0 s is 3.0 m s^-1, the velocity at t = 4.0 s is also 3.0 m s^-1.
The velocity at t = 4.0 s is 24 m s^-1, because the position-time graph is at 24 m at that instant.
The velocity at t = 4.0 s is 48 m s^-1, the area under the position-time graph between t = 0 and t = 4.0 s.
The velocity at t = 4.0 s is 24 divided by 4.0, that is 6.0 m s^-1.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Is acceleration being determined from change in velocity per unit time, with the correct sign?
units.mechanism: Average acceleration is Delta v / Delta t; instantaneous acceleration is a = dv/dt, the slope of the tangent to the velocity-time graph at that instant.

mx.cwo: The acceleration at t = 2 s is 4 m s^-2, because the velocity rose from 0 to 40 m s^-1 over the whole 10 s of the trip.
A car going round a bend at a steady 40 km/h has zero acceleration, because its velocity is not changing.
The acceleration at t = 4.0 s is 3.8 m s^-2, read off as the slope of the position-time graph at that instant.
A car slowing from 20 m s^-1 to 10 m s^-1 in 5 s has an acceleration of +2 m s^-2.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Do the signs of velocity and acceleration correctly predict motion direction, slowing down, speeding up, or turning back?
units.mechanism: For constant acceleration, v = v0 + at; the sign of velocity gives direction along the chosen axis, while acceleration changes velocity with time.

mx.cwo: The car's speed is -15 m s^-1, which shows that it is moving in the negative direction.
A body moving in the negative direction cannot have a positive acceleration, because the only cases are positive with positive, positive with negative and negative with negative.
The velocity-time line slopes downward for the whole 10 s, so the body slows down the whole time and is slowest at t = 10 s.
A ball thrown up with velocity +20 m s^-1 under a = -10 m s^-2 is still moving in the positive direction at t = 5 s, at 20 m s^-1.

A copper bar is a fluid because it changes its shape when a large enough shear force is applied to it.

Mercury is too dense to be a fluid; only light substances such as water and air count as fluids.

mx.cwo: The relative density of mercury is 13.6 g cm^-3.
The air in a bicycle pump stays at 1.2 kg m^-3 while the piston is pushed in, because the density of a substance is a fixed property of that substance.
A 2 m^3 block of pine has a greater density than a 0.5 m^3 block cut from the same log.
A gas has no density, because it has no volume of its own to divide the mass by.
The density of a 2 kg block occupying 0.5 m^3 is 0.5/2 = 0.25 kg m^-3.

A brick of weight 20 N standing on its narrow 0.002 m^2 end exerts 20/0.008 = 2500 Pa, using the area of its largest face.
A 600 N block resting on its 0.5 m^2 face exerts more pressure on the floor than the same block resting on its 0.01 m^2 face.
The 500 N push produces more pressure than the 20 N push, whatever areas the two forces act over.
P = 0.20/50 = 0.004 Pa for a 50 N normal force acting on 0.20 m^2.

units.decision_hinge: In a fluid at rest, decide that pressure at a point has no direction and is the same in all directions and at the same height.
units.mechanism: In a fluid at rest, pressure is the same at all points at the same height and is exerted equally in all directions; the force on any surface is normal to that surface.

mx.cwo: At the same depth in a tank the water pushes on a 2 cm^2 plate and on a 20 cm^2 plate with the same force, because it is the same in all directions.
In a horizontal pipe carrying flowing water, the pressure in the wide section equals the pressure in the narrow section because both are at the same height.
A beaker of water and a beaker of mercury stand side by side on a bench; at 5 cm above the bench the pressure in the two liquids is the same.
A and B lie on the same slanting line drawn across the vessel, so the pressure at A equals the pressure at B.
The pressure at the bottom of a 5 m deep open tank is 1.0 x 10^5 Pa, the same as at the surface, because pressure applied to a fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout it.

units.decision_hinge: For a point below an open liquid surface, choose P = P_a + rho g h for absolute pressure and rho g h for gauge pressure, independent of container shape.
units.mechanism: In a liquid at rest with uniform density, pressure at depth h below an open surface is P = P_a + rho g h; the excess pressure P - P_a is gauge pressure.

The lower end of a 10 m tube inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal, filled with water from an open top, is at a gauge pressure of 9.8 x 10^4 Pa.
In a sealed can with vacuum above the liquid, the absolute pressure 2 m below the surface is 1.2 x 10^5 Pa, because atmospheric pressure is always added.
The gauge pressure at the base of the conical flask is the weight of the water it holds divided by the base area, 3.6 x 10^3 Pa.

units.decision_hinge: When a barometer or U-tube is used, equate pressures at the same level and convert liquid-column height into pressure with rho g h.
units.mechanism: Atmospheric pressure can be represented by rho g h for a liquid column, and pressure is the same at the same level on both sides of a connected U-tube containing a fluid.

In a U-tube holding water in one arm and oil in the other, the two free surfaces must stand at the same level because pressure is equal at equal levels.
Since mercury is 13.6 times denser than water, a water barometer at the same atmospheric pressure would stand only about 0.06 m high.
Atmospheric pressure from the barometer is 76 Pa, read straight off the centimetre mark reached by the mercury.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: In a hydraulic lift or brake, transmit the applied pressure unchanged through the enclosed fluid, then use piston area to find force and displacement.
units.mechanism: A change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid. In a hydraulic lift, P = F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2, so F_2 = F_1 A_2/A_1, while incompressible volume displacement gives L_1 A_1 = L_2 A_2.

mx.cwo: A 50 N push on the small piston appears as 50 N at the large piston, because the force is transmitted undiminished through the fluid.
A hydraulic lift filled with air instead of oil multiplies a 50 N push into 500 N at the large piston in exactly the same way.
With A_1 = 10 cm^2 and A_2 = 100 cm^2, a 50 N push on the small piston produces 5 N at the large piston.
The large piston is 3 times the diameter of the small one, so a 50 N push lifts 150 N.
Because the same volume of oil passes each second, the large piston rises faster than the small piston is pushed down.

units.decision_hinge: For steady incompressible flow through a changing cross-section, keep the volume flow rate A v constant and predict higher speed in narrower regions.

Steam entering a section of pipe with one quarter the area must speed up exactly four times, even though it is being compressed on the way in.
A river narrowing to one third of its width through rapids must flow exactly three times faster there, with the same smooth streamline pattern.
The wide section of the pipe carries the water faster, because you can see far more water moving through it every second.

units.decision_hinge: Along a streamline of ideal steady flow, trade pressure, kinetic energy per unit volume, and gravitational potential energy per unit volume so their sum stays constant.
units.mechanism: Bernoulli's equation is P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline for steady incompressible flow without energy loss due to friction.

The pressure drop along a 20 m horizontal pipe of constant bore carrying oil at a steady speed is zero, because v and h are unchanged.
Bernoulli's equation cannot be used for the water standing still in a closed tank, because there is no flow for the equation to describe.
At the narrow section 2 m below the tank surface the pressure is 1.0 x 10^5 + 1000 x 9.8 x 2 = 1.2 x 10^5 Pa, because pressure in a liquid depends only on depth.
For water at 4 m/s the kinetic term is (1/2) rho v = 0.5 x 1000 x 4 = 2000 Pa.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For efflux from a tank, decide whether the exit speed is sqrt(2 g h) or must include the pressure-head term.
units.mechanism: For efflux, Bernoulli's equation gives v_1 = sqrt(2 g h + 2(P - P_a)/rho). If the tank is open to the atmosphere and the top area is much larger than the hole, this reduces to v_1 = sqrt(2 g h).

mx.cwo: For a hole 1 m above the floor in a tank filled to a depth of 5 m, the water emerges at sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 1) = 4.4 m/s.
A closed tank with gas at 3 x 10^5 Pa above the water gives an efflux speed of sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 2) = 6.3 m/s at a hole 2 m below the surface.
Moving the hole from 2 m to 4 m below the surface doubles the jet speed from 6.3 m/s to 12.6 m/s.
With the tank cross-section 100 times the hole area and the surface dropping at 0.01 m/s, the water leaves the hole at 1 m/s whatever the 2 m depth is.
For a hole 2 m below the surface, v = 2 g h = 2 x 9.8 x 2 = 39.2 m/s.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a spinning ball or aerofoil, infer lift from the pressure difference created by unequal air speeds on opposite sides.
units.mechanism: Dynamic lift arises when unequal fluid speeds on opposite sides of a moving body create a pressure difference; for an aircraft wing, the pressure difference times wing area supplies the upward lift.

mx.cwo: Lift = pressure difference x wing span = 500 x 12 = 6000 N.
A smooth cricket ball bowled without any spin still swerves sideways in flight, because air moving past a ball always produces dynamic lift.
A ball given topspin swerves upwards and stays in the air longer than a ball with no spin.
A flat rectangular plate held in an airstream can produce no lift at all, because it has no curved upper surface.
The aircraft stays up because it displaces its own weight of air, so a bigger aircraft floats in the air just as a bigger boat floats in water.
