units.mechanism: The coefficient of viscosity is eta = (F/A)/(v/l) = F l/(v A), the ratio of shearing stress to strain rate in a flowing fluid.

mx.cwo: eta = (F/A)/(x/l), the shearing stress divided by the shear strain, so viscosity is measured in pascals.
The viscosity of the air inside a hot oven is lower than that of the air in a cold room, because heating always makes a fluid flow more easily.
Doubling the force on the plate doubles the coefficient of viscosity of the oil, from 1.0 Pa s to 2.0 Pa s.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a small sphere moving through a viscous fluid, use Stokes' drag and balance forces to determine terminal velocity.
units.mechanism: Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a sphere as F = 6 pi eta a v. For a sphere falling through a fluid, terminal velocity is v_t = 2 a^2 (rho - sigma) g/(9 eta).

mx.cwo: For a ball bearing of diameter 2 mm, the viscous drag is F = 6 pi eta (0.002) v.
At terminal speed, 6 pi eta a v_t = (4/3) pi a^3 rho g, so the density of the liquid does not enter the answer.
A cricket ball of radius 3.6 cm falling through air has terminal speed 2a^2(rho - sigma)g/(9 eta), about 1.9 x 10^4 m/s.
The drag on the sphere is eta A v/l with A its cross-sectional area, so F = eta pi a^2 v/l.
v_t = 2a(rho - sigma)g/(9 eta), so halving the radius of the sphere halves its terminal speed.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: At a liquid interface, treat surface tension as force per unit length and surface energy per unit area, including the two-surface factor for a film.
units.mechanism: Surface tension is the force per unit length, or surface energy per unit area, acting in the plane of an interface. For a liquid film with two surfaces, S = F/(2 l); in the plate method, S_la = mg/(2 l).

mx.cwo: S = F/A, the force divided by the surface area of the film, so surface tension is measured in N m^-2.
A soap film on a frame with a 10 cm movable bar held by a force of 0.0015 N gives S = 0.0015/0.10 = 0.015 N/m.
The surface tension at a water-oil interface is 0.073 N/m, the same as at the water-air surface, because surface tension is a property of water.
S = 2F/l = 2 x 0.0015/0.10 = 0.030 N/m for a 10 cm bar held by 0.0015 N.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use liquid-air, solid-air, and solid-liquid surface tensions to decide whether a liquid spreads on a solid or forms droplets.
units.mechanism: At the line of contact, the interfacial tensions satisfy S_la cos theta + S_sl = S_sa. The angle of contact determines whether a liquid spreads on a solid surface or forms droplets.

mx.cwo: cos theta = (S_sl - S_sa)/S_la, so water on clean glass has an obtuse contact angle.
Water has a contact angle of about zero on every solid, so water spreads on wax and on a lotus leaf just as it does on clean glass.
Water beads up into droplets on clean glass because water molecules are strongly attracted to glass.
A large puddle of water on wax spreads out, so water does wet wax; only very small drops of it bead up.
Mercury spreads on glass more than water does, because mercury has the larger surface tension, 0.465 N/m against 0.073 N/m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For drops, air bubbles in liquid, and soap bubbles, choose the correct excess pressure from curvature and the number of liquid-air interfaces.
units.mechanism: For a spherical drop or one liquid-gas interface, P_i - P_o = 2 S/r; for a soap bubble with two interfaces, P_i - P_o = 4 S/r. The concave side of a curved liquid-gas interface has the higher pressure.

mx.cwo: The pressure inside an air bubble of radius 1 mm in water is 146 Pa.
A soap bubble of radius 5 cm hanging from a ring stays exactly spherical and has the same excess pressure 4S/r at every point of its surface.
When a large soap bubble and a small one are joined by a tube, air flows from the large bubble into the small one because the larger bubble holds the greater pressure.
An air bubble trapped under water in a soapy tank has excess pressure 4S/r, because it is a soap bubble.
The excess pressure inside a bubble 0.5 m below the water surface is rho g h = 4.9 x 10^3 Pa.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For capillary action, combine meniscus curvature with hydrostatic balance to determine whether the liquid rises or falls and by how much.
units.mechanism: Capillary rise satisfies h rho g = 2 S cos theta/a, so h = 2 S cos theta/(rho g a); when cos theta is negative for a convex meniscus, the liquid level is lower in the capillary.

mx.cwo: For a capillary of diameter 0.5 mm, h = 2S cos theta/(rho g x 0.0005) = 0.03 m.
Water in a very long fine capillary keeps climbing as long as the tube is long enough, so a 3 m tube of that bore can lift water to its top.
Water rises higher in a tube of radius 1 mm than in one of radius 0.2 mm, because the wider tube can hold a taller column.
Water cannot rise through the pores of blotting paper by capillary action, because capillary rise needs a narrow glass tube.
Pushing the capillary tube deeper into the water makes the water climb higher inside the tube.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a situation is describing temperature as hotness or heat as energy transfer caused by a temperature difference.
units.mechanism: Temperature represents the degree of hotness of a body, while heat is energy transferred between systems or between a system and its surroundings because their temperatures differ.

mx.cwo: Rubbing two blocks that are both at 30 degree C transfers 50 J of heat from one block to the other.
Two blocks both at 30 degree C placed in contact go on exchanging heat, and the larger block ends up hotter.
A bath of water at 30 degree C transfers heat to a cup of water at 80 degree C, because the bath contains far more heat.
Energy arriving at the Earth from the Sun is not heat, because heat can only pass between bodies that are touching.
The tea is losing heat while steam rises from it; once the steam stops, no more heat is leaving the cup.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Convert temperatures by treating Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin scales as fixed-point linear scales, not as proportional labels.
units.mechanism: Celsius and Fahrenheit readings are related by (t_F - 32)/180 = t_C/100, so t_F = (9/5)t_C + 32; Kelvin and Celsius have equal unit size and are related by T = t_c + 273.15.

mx.cwo: t_F = (5/9)t_C + 32, so 100 degree C is 87.6 degree F.
25 degree C converts to 45 degree F, because one Celsius degree is 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees.
A rise of 20 degree C is a rise of 293 K.
77 degree F = (77 x 5/9) - 32 = 10.8 degree C.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use the ideal-gas relation with absolute temperature when pressure, volume, amount of gas, and temperature are connected.
units.mechanism: For a given amount of ideal gas, PV/T is constant and the general relation is PV = mu RT; for constant volume gas thermometry, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.

mx.cwo: For 2 g of helium at 300 K in 5 litres, P = mu RT/V with mu = 2 gives P = 9.98 x 10^5 Pa.
As air is pumped into a tyre of fixed volume, PV/T stays constant, so tripling the pressure must triple the absolute temperature.
Cooling one mole of nitrogen to 20 K at 1 atm shrinks it to 1.6 litres exactly as PV = mu RT predicts, and at 0 K its volume becomes zero.
Heating the air in a balloon from 300 K to 330 K increases its volume by alpha_v Delta T with alpha_v = 3.6 x 10^-5 per degree, that is by about 0.1 percent.
P_1 V_1 T_1 = P_2 V_2 T_2, so doubling the absolute temperature of a gas at fixed volume halves its pressure.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Predict whether heating or cooling changes a body's dimensions, while recognizing water's 0 degree C to 4 degree C exception and the larger expansion of gases.
units.mechanism: Most substances expand on heating and contract on cooling; water contracts on heating between 0 degree C and 4 degree C and has maximum density at 4 degree C, while gases at ordinary temperature expand much more than solids and liquids.

mx.cwo: Water has its lowest density at 4 degree C, which is why a pond freezes from the bottom upwards.
A sealed rigid steel cylinder of gas heated from 300 K to 330 K expands by ten percent.
When the steel washer is heated its 10.00 mm hole shrinks to 9.99 mm, because the steel expands inwards into the hole.
Only the mercury in a thermometer expands when it is heated; the glass bulb keeps exactly the same volume.
Water warmed from 0 degree C to 4 degree C shows no change in volume at all, because all the heat supplied over that range is being used up in melting.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Choose the correct linear, area, or volume expansion relation for a small temperature change.
units.mechanism: For small temperature changes, Delta l/l = alpha_l Delta T and Delta V/V = alpha_v Delta T; for an isotropic solid expanding equally in all directions, alpha_v = 3 alpha_l and the area expansion coefficient is approximately 2 alpha_l.

mx.cwo: A steel rod heated through 50 degree C lengthens by alpha_l Delta T = 6 x 10^-4 m, whether it is 1 m or 10 m long.
The volume expansivity of wood is three times its linear expansivity along the grain, since alpha_v is always 3 alpha_l.
The linear expansivity of glycerine is alpha_v/3 = 1.6 x 10^-4 per degree C.
For copper with alpha_v = 4.95 x 10^-5 per degree C, alpha_l = 3 x 4.95 x 10^-5 = 1.49 x 10^-4 per degree C.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Account for thermal stress when a solid is prevented from expanding or contracting freely.
units.mechanism: If a rod's thermal expansion is prevented by rigid supports, the would-be thermal strain alpha_l Delta T becomes mechanical strain and produces stress equal to Young's modulus times that strain.

mx.cwo: The thermal stress in the clamped steel rod heated through 100 degree C is alpha_l Delta T = 1.2 x 10^-3 Pa.
A steel rail lying free on the sleepers and heated through 30 degree C develops a compressive stress of Y alpha_l Delta T = 7.2 x 10^7 Pa.
A rod clamped between two rigid walls and then heated is put under tension, so it is stretched and may snap in hot weather.
A steel rail develops no thermal stress when it is heated, because steel is far too strong to be deformed by a 30 degree C rise.
The clamped 1 m steel rod heated through 30 degree C grows 0.36 mm longer and pushes the walls apart by that amount.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use specific heat capacity or molar specific heat capacity to connect heat transfer, amount of substance, and temperature change when no phase change occurs.
units.mechanism: Heat needed for a temperature change depends on mass, the temperature change, and the substance: s = (1/m)(Delta Q/Delta T), and C = (1/mu)(Delta Q/Delta T) for molar specific heat capacity.

mx.cwo: A 2 kg block needing 1600 J to rise 10 degree C has a specific heat capacity of 160 J K^-1.
Supplying 3.35 x 10^5 J to 1 kg of ice at 0 degree C raises its temperature by Q/(m s) = 160 degree C.
Water has a higher specific heat capacity than iron, so 1 kg of water given 1000 J rises through a larger temperature change than 1 kg of iron.
A metal spoon has a low specific heat capacity because it feels cold, while a wooden spoon at the same temperature has a high one.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Set up calorimetry by equating heat lost by hotter parts to heat gained by colder parts within an isolated system.
units.mechanism: In an isolated calorimetry system, when bodies at different temperatures reach a steady final temperature, heat lost by the hotter body equals heat gained by the colder body and the calorimeter.

mx.cwo: The 0.05 kg copper calorimeter absorbs 0.05 x 4186 x Delta T joules.
Heat lost by the aluminium equals heat gained by the water alone, so the final temperature of the mixture is 29.6 degree C.
Mixing 0.5 kg of water at 20 degree C with 0.1 kg of water at 80 degree C gives a final temperature of 68 degree C, because the larger mass of cold water changes temperature more.
The final temperature must lie closer to 100 degree C than to 20 degree C, because 100 is the larger of the two readings.
The final temperature of the mixture is 25 degree C, the temperature of the laboratory, because the hot body keeps losing heat until it reaches the surroundings.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Separate a heating or cooling process into temperature-change segments and phase-change plateaus, using latent heat only during change of state.
units.mechanism: During a change of state, added or removed heat changes phase while temperature remains constant; the heat for that part is Q = mL, while single-phase temperature changes use Q = ms Delta T.

mx.cwo: Melting 1 kg of ice at 0 degree C requires 2.26 x 10^6 J.
Heating 1 kg of water from 60 degree C to 80 degree C requires mL = 2.26 x 10^6 J, because water is turning into steam as it warms.
Water on a mountain top boils at 100 degree C, so the flat part of its heating curve is at 100 degree C whatever the pressure is.
Steam at 100 degree C and boiling water at 100 degree C carry exactly the same energy, because the thermometer reads the same in both.
Warming 1 kg of ice at -10 degree C to water at 20 degree C needs 4186 x 30 plus mL, that is 4.6 x 10^5 J.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use pressure-temperature phase information to predict boiling, sublimation, and triple-point behavior.
units.mechanism: The temperature of a substance remains constant during phase change, and a pressure-temperature phase diagram separates solid, liquid, and vapour regions; pressure changes can change the boiling point.

mx.cwo: The triple point of water is at 100 degree C and 1 atm, the conditions at which all three states coexist.
Water boiling at reduced pressure at 80 degree C goes on boiling indefinitely at 80 degree C without any heat being supplied to it.
On a high mountain where the pressure is low, water boils at about 120 degree C, which is why cooking there is slow.
Solid carbon dioxide must melt into a liquid before it can become a gas, since every substance passes through all three states in turn.
The water in the beaker at 60 degree C is boiling, because bubbles are rising through it.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Classify a heat-transfer situation as conduction, convection, or radiation from the carrier of energy transfer.
units.mechanism: Heat transfer occurs by conduction through neighboring parts without matter flow, by convection through actual motion of matter in fluids, and by radiation through electromagnetic energy that can cross vacuum.

mx.cwo: Heat travels from the Sun to the Earth by convection, since the hot gases carry the energy across space.
Heat travels along an iron bar by convection, because the hot particles move from the hot end to the cold end.
A person at 37 degree C emits no thermal radiation at all, because only objects hot enough to glow can radiate.
Heat crosses the air gap of a double-glazed window by conduction, at a small rate because air has a low thermal conductivity.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Calculate steady-state conductive heat current through a bar or compound bar using geometry, thermal conductivity, and temperature difference.
units.mechanism: In steady one-dimensional conduction through a uniform bar, H = K A (T_C - T_D)/L; larger K, area, or temperature difference increases heat current, and larger length decreases it.

mx.cwo: The heat conducted through the copper bar is H = K A Delta T/L = 51 J.
The instant a 100 degree C flame is applied to one end of a 1 m iron bar, the far end starts receiving heat at K A Delta T/L = 3.7 W.
Doubling the length of the copper bar doubles the heat current through it, because there is twice as much copper to carry the heat.
No heat at all is conducted through the wooden handle of the pan, because only metals conduct heat.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Explain natural and forced convection from fluid motion, temperature differences, and gravity-driven circulation.
units.mechanism: Convection transfers heat by actual motion of matter in fluids; natural convection depends on gravity when unequal temperatures create circulating motion, while forced convection uses an external pump or other physical means.

mx.cwo: The circulation of water in a beaker heated from below is forced convection, because the heating forces the water to move.
A candle burning in an orbiting spacecraft sets up the same upward convection currents and burns with the same tapering upward flame as on Earth.
During the day the breeze blows from the land out to the sea, because the hot land pushes the air away from itself.
Water at the bottom of a beaker warms the water above it purely by passing heat from layer to layer, so the top warms last and nothing circulates.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Predict how surface colour, reflectivity, and vacuum insulation affect radiative heat transfer.
units.mechanism: Radiation can transfer heat without a material medium; black bodies absorb and emit radiant energy better than lighter-coloured bodies, while shiny reflecting surfaces and evacuated spaces reduce heat transfer.

mx.cwo: A matt black kettle absorbs radiation well but gives it out poorly, so it stays hot longer than a shiny one.
A black metal spoon conducts heat to your hand faster than an identical white one, because black absorbs heat better.
Tea in a Dewar flask stays at 90 degree C indefinitely, because the vacuum and the silvering remove every path by which heat could leave.
A black-painted aluminium sheet reflects radiation just as bare aluminium does, because it is still metal underneath the paint.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use Wien's displacement law to relate a blackbody's peak wavelength or observed colour to its temperature.
units.mechanism: For blackbody radiation, the wavelength lambda_m of maximum emitted energy decreases as temperature increases, with lambda_m T equal to a constant of 2.9 x 10^-3 m K.

mx.cwo: The frequency of maximum emission times the absolute temperature equals 2.9 x 10^-3, so a hotter body peaks at a lower frequency.
A body at 27 degree C has lambda_m = 2.9 x 10^-3/27 = 1.1 x 10^-4 m.
A red car is cooler than a blue car standing beside it, because red light has the longer wavelength.
The large bonfire must be hotter than the small blowtorch flame, because it is far bigger and brighter.
Doubling the absolute temperature makes the peak wavelength sixteen times shorter, because radiation goes as the fourth power of temperature.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use Stefan-Boltzmann relations to calculate total or net radiative power from area, emissivity, and absolute temperatures.
units.mechanism: The total energy radiated per unit time is H = A sigma T^4 for a perfect radiator and H = A e sigma T^4 for emissivity e; with surroundings at T_s, net loss is H = e sigma A (T^4 - T_s^4).

mx.cwo: The net rate at which the body loses heat is e sigma A T^4 = 858 W, using its own temperature alone.
For a body at 28 degree C with A = 1.9 m^2 and e = 0.97, H = e sigma A (28)^4 = 0.064 W.
Human skin at 307 K radiates A sigma T^4 with e = 1, because every hot body is a perfect radiator.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Apply Newton's law of cooling to predict cooling rate or cooling time from excess temperature over the surroundings.
units.mechanism: For small temperature differences, the rate of heat loss is proportional to the excess temperature of the body over the surroundings: -dQ/dt = k(T_2 - T_1), leading to log_e(T_2 - T_1) = -Kt + c and T_2 = T_1 + C' e^(-Kt).

mx.cwo: A body at 80 degree C in a 20 degree C room loses heat at a rate proportional to 80, so -dQ/dt = 80k.
Molten iron at 1500 degree C in a 20 degree C room cools according to -dQ/dt = k(1500 - 20) with the same k measured for a cup of tea.
Tea in a wide shallow dish and tea in a narrow flask cool at exactly the same rate, because cooling depends only on the temperature difference.
Tea at 353 K cools 1.6 times faster than the same tea at 313 K, because the rate goes as the fourth power of its temperature.
log_e(80) - log_e(20) = -K t, so the cooling constant is found from the ratio of the two body temperatures.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a thermodynamic system is in equilibrium from the behavior of its macroscopic variables and its contact with the surroundings.
units.mechanism: A thermodynamic equilibrium state is one in which the macroscopic variables characterising the system do not change in time; whether equilibrium is reached depends on the surroundings and on the wall separating the system from them.

mx.cwo: thermodynamic system still holds here even though Use macroscopic variables such as pressure, volume, temperature, mass, and composition is missing from the stem.
Surroundings is what produces thermodynamic system, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The thermodynamic system rule also covers this: The system must be considered together with its surroundings and constraints, so it is not an exception.
thermodynamic system is settled by running 'Decide whether a process is reversible or irreversible by checking': A process is reversible only if it can be reversed so that both the system and the.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide when two systems are in thermal equilibrium and how the Zeroth Law introduces temperature.
units.mechanism: In thermal equilibrium, two systems have equal temperature. If two systems are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

mx.cwo: System B is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Decide when two systems are in thermal equilibrium and how the Zeroth' is answered as system B rather than system A.
system A still holds here even though The comparison is about thermal equilibrium, not mechanical equilibrium is missing from the stem.
System B is what produces system A, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The system A rule also covers this: Equal temperature is the diagnostic quantity, even if other variables such as pressure need not both change, so it is not an exception.

The answer is system A because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Decide when two systems are in thermal equilibrium and how the Zeroth' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish internal energy from heat and work when describing energy changes of a system.
units.mechanism: Internal energy is a state variable of the system, while heat and work are distinct modes of energy transfer that can change internal energy and are not state variables.

mx.cwo: Heat is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Distinguish internal energy from heat and work when describing energy' is answered as heat rather than internal energy.
internal energy still holds here even though Heat is energy in transit; it is not energy stored inside a body as a state property is missing from the stem.

The answer is internal energy because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Distinguish internal energy from heat and work when describing energy' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Apply the First Law with the chapter's sign convention for heat supplied to the system and work done by the system.
units.mechanism: With Delta Q as heat supplied to the system and Delta W as work done by the system, conservation of energy gives Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, or Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W.

mx.cwo: Delta U is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Apply the First Law with the chapter's sign convention for heat' is answered as Delta U rather than Delta Q.

The answer is Delta Q because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Apply the First Law with the chapter's sign convention for heat' as the operative test.
Delta Q is settled by running 'Choose the appropriate heat-capacity relation from heat capacity': Heat capacity is S = Delta Q / Delta T, specific heat capacity is s = (1/m)(Delta Q /.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Calculate the internal-energy change when heat supplied and expansion work are both present.
units.mechanism: For a constant-pressure expansion, the work done by the system is P Delta V and the internal-energy change is Delta U = Delta Q - P Delta V.

mx.cwo: Expansion work is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Calculate the internal-energy change when heat supplied and expansion' is answered as expansion work rather than constant pressure.
Expansion work is what produces constant pressure, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.

The answer is constant pressure because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Calculate the internal-energy change when heat supplied and expansion' as the operative test.
constant pressure is settled by running 'Choose the appropriate heat-capacity relation from heat capacity': Heat capacity is S = Delta Q / Delta T, specific heat capacity is s = (1/m)(Delta Q /.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Choose the appropriate heat-capacity relation from heat capacity, specific heat capacity, and molar specific heat capacity.
units.mechanism: Heat capacity is S = Delta Q / Delta T, specific heat capacity is s = (1/m)(Delta Q / Delta T), and molar specific heat capacity is C = (1/mu)(Delta Q / Delta T).

mx.cwo: Specific heat capacity is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Choose the appropriate heat-capacity relation from heat capacity' is answered as specific heat capacity rather than heat capacity.
heat capacity still holds here even though Use mass m when the quantity is specified in kilograms and use number of moles mu when the is missing from the stem.
Specific heat capacity is what produces heat capacity, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The heat capacity rule also covers this: For gases, heat capacity depends on the process or conditions, such as constant pressure or constant volume, so it is not an exception.

The answer is heat capacity because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Choose the appropriate heat-capacity relation from heat capacity' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use the solid and ideal-gas heat-capacity constraints only under the conditions in which the chapter derives them.
units.mechanism: For a solid at ordinary temperatures with negligible volume change, the molar heat capacity is approximately C = 3R; for an ideal gas, the molar heat capacities satisfy Cp - Cv = R.

mx.cwo: Ordinary temperature is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Use the solid and ideal-gas heat-capacity constraints only under the' is answered as ordinary temperature rather than solid.
Ordinary temperature is what produces solid, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
solid is settled by running 'Use the Second Law to rule out processes that conserve energy but have': No process can have as its sole result the absorption of heat from a reservoir and.
Solid is computed by squaring ordinary temperature and leaving solid linear, so the written value is 89.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Identify state variables and use an equation of state to decide how many independent variables describe an equilibrium gas.
units.mechanism: Equilibrium states are described by state variables, whose values depend only on the state; for an ideal gas, PV = mu RT connects pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas.

mx.cwo: Equilibrium state is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Identify state variables and use an equation of state to decide how' is answered as equilibrium state rather than state variable.
Equilibrium state is what produces state variable, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.

state variable is settled by running 'Distinguish internal energy from heat and work when describing energy': Internal energy is a state variable of the system, while heat and work are distinct modes.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a thermodynamic process can be treated as quasi-static.
units.mechanism: A quasi-static process is an idealised, infinitely slow process in which the system remains in thermal and mechanical equilibrium with the surroundings throughout.

mx.cwo: quasi-static process still holds here even though The process must be slow enough that the system remains near equilibrium at every stage is missing from the stem.
Thermal equilibrium is what produces quasi-static process, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The quasi-static process rule also covers this: The pressure and temperature of the system are well defined at every stage of a quasi-static process, so it is not an exception.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Classify a process as isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, or adiabatic from the quantity held fixed or the heat-flow condition.
units.mechanism: An isothermal process has constant temperature, an isobaric process has constant pressure, an isochoric process has constant volume, and an adiabatic process has no heat flow between system and surroundings.

mx.cwo: Isobaric process is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Classify a process as isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, or adiabatic' is answered as isobaric process rather than isothermal process.
Isobaric process is what produces isothermal process, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.

isothermal process is settled by running 'Apply the isothermal ideal-gas model to relate pressure, volume, heat': For an isothermal process of an ideal gas, temperature is fixed, PV is constant, internal.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Apply the isothermal ideal-gas model to relate pressure, volume, heat, work, and internal energy.
units.mechanism: For an isothermal process of an ideal gas, temperature is fixed, PV is constant, internal energy does not change, and Q = W = mu R T ln(V2/V1).

mx.cwo: Ideal gas is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Apply the isothermal ideal-gas model to relate pressure, volume, heat' is answered as ideal gas rather than isothermal process.
isothermal process still holds here even though The gas must be treated as an ideal gas at fixed temperature is missing from the stem.

The answer is isothermal process because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Apply the isothermal ideal-gas model to relate pressure, volume, heat' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Apply the adiabatic ideal-gas model to connect pressure, volume, work, and temperature change.
units.mechanism: For an adiabatic process of an ideal gas, heat absorbed or released is zero, PV^gamma is constant, gamma = Cp/Cv, and W = mu R(T1 - T2)/(gamma - 1).

mx.cwo: Ideal gas is the label that belongs on this item, so 'Apply the adiabatic ideal-gas model to connect pressure, volume, work' is answered as ideal gas rather than adiabatic process.
adiabatic process still holds here even though The system must be insulated from the surroundings so that heat absorbed or released is is missing from the stem.
Ideal gas is what produces adiabatic process, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The adiabatic process rule also covers this: The sign of work must follow whether work is done by the gas or on the gas, so it is not an exception.

The answer is adiabatic process because of the most obvious label, colour, size or printed number in the stem, without using 'Apply the adiabatic ideal-gas model to connect pressure, volume, work' as the operative test.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Apply the special consequences of isochoric, isobaric, and cyclic processes.
units.mechanism: In an isochoric process no work is done; in an isobaric process W = P(V2 - V1) = mu R(T2 - T1); in a cyclic process Delta U = 0, so the total heat absorbed equals the work done by the system.

mx.cwo: isochoric process still holds here even though The no-work result for an isochoric process requires constant volume is missing from the stem.
Isobaric process is what produces isochoric process, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards.
The isochoric process rule also covers this: The cyclic-process result Delta U = 0 requires the final state to be the same as the initial state, so it is not an exception.
isochoric process is settled by running 'Calculate the internal-energy change when heat supplied and expansion': For a constant-pressure expansion, the work done by the system is P Delta V and the.
Isochoric process is computed by squaring isobaric process and leaving isochoric process linear, so the written value is 51.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use the Second Law to rule out processes that conserve energy but have impossible heat-flow or work-conversion results.

A 5 nC charge placed in the cavity of an uncharged metal shell produces no field outside the shell, because the cavity is shielded.
The electric field inside a solid wooden block placed between charged plates is zero, because the field cannot get inside a solid object.
Inside the metal slab the field is E_0/K rather than zero, since the slab polarises like any other material.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Explain how a dielectric in an external electric field polarises and why that changes the net field and capacitance.
units.mechanism: A dielectric develops a net dipole moment in an external electric field; for linear dielectrics P = epsilon_0*chi_e*E, induced surface charge produces a field opposing the original field, and a fully inserted dielectric gives C = epsilon_0*K*A/d with K > 1.

mx.cwo: Water is a non-polar dielectric, so it polarises only by displacement of its charge centres and carries no permanent dipole moment.
Sliding a 2 mm slab of K = 4 into a 5 mm gap gives C = epsilon_0 K A/d = 4 C_0.
Inserting a dielectric of K = 4 raises the field between the plates, so the potential difference rises and the capacitance falls to C_0/4.
The thicker glass slab has the larger dielectric constant, so it raises the capacitance more than the thin one does.
The net electric field inside the dielectric slab is zero, because the induced surface charges cancel the applied field exactly.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Use capacitance as a property of a conductor pair, not as the instantaneous charge or voltage alone, and derive the parallel-plate result from field and geometry.
units.mechanism: Capacitance is C = Q/V and is independent of Q and V for a given capacitor; for parallel plates with plate area A and separation d in vacuum or air, E = Q/(epsilon_0*A), V = Ed = Qd/(epsilon_0*A), and C = epsilon_0*A/d.

mx.cwo: For two 2 cm square plates held 5 cm apart, C = epsilon_0 A/d = 7.1 x 10^-14 F exactly.
Doubling the plate separation from 1 mm to 2 mm doubles the capacitance of the capacitor.
Raising the voltage on a 1 uF air capacitor to 10^6 V stores Q = CV = 1 C on its plates.
The capacitor with the bigger plates has the larger capacitance, whatever the size of the gap between them.
The potential difference between plates carrying 2 nC and separated by 1 mm is V = kQ/d = 1.8 x 10^4 V.
For A = 100 cm^2 and d = 1 mm, C = epsilon_0 d/A = 8.9 x 10^-13 F.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a capacitor network, decide which capacitors share charge and which share voltage before finding equivalent capacitance and individual charges.
units.mechanism: In series, the same charge Q appears on each capacitor and the potential drops add, giving V = Q/C1 + Q/C2 and 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2, with the same reasoning extending to any number in series. In parallel, branches connected across the same terminals share the same potential difference and their capacitances add in the worked network.

mx.cwo: C2 and C3, drawn side by side in the diagram, add directly to give 20 uF.
The three 10 uF capacitors on one branch are in parallel and give 30 uF, while C4 across the same two terminals is in series with them.
In the bridge network the equivalent capacitance is 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3 + 1/C4, since all four capacitors lie between A and D.
C1 and C4 are both marked 10 uF, so they must carry the same charge in the network.
Three 10 uF capacitors in series give 1/C = 0.3, so C = 0.3 uF.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Choose the correct energy expression for a charged capacitor or for the electric field region, and track what is conserved when capacitors are reconnected.
units.mechanism: The energy stored in a capacitor is U = Q^2/(2C) = (1/2)CV^2 = (1/2)QV; the electric energy density is u = (1/2)epsilon_0*E^2.

mx.cwo: The energy density between the plates is u = (1/2) epsilon_0 V^2, so at 100 V it is 4.4 x 10^-8 J/m^3.
Doubling the voltage on a capacitor from 100 V to 200 V doubles its stored energy from 4.5 uJ to 9 uJ.
The space around an isolated point charge stores no energy, because u = (1/2) epsilon_0 E^2 applies only between capacitor plates.
For a 900 pF capacitor carrying 9 x 10^-8 C, U = C^2/(2Q) = 4.5 x 10^-12 J.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether current through a chosen area should be treated as signed net charge per unit time, and use an instantaneous limit when the flow is not steady.
units.mechanism: For a chosen forward direction, steady current is I = q/t; in general I(t) = lim_{Delta t -> 0} Delta Q/Delta t. A negative value means the current is in the opposite direction, and current is a scalar even when an arrow marks the chosen direction.

mx.cwo: In the electrolyte 2 C of negative ions cross to the right and 2 C of positive ions cross to the left each second, so the current is 2 A.
Charge 6 C crosses the section in 3 s while the flow is speeding up, so the current at the end of the 3 s is 2 A.
Both branches carry +2 A because both arrows in the figure are drawn pointing away from the junction.
Two 3 A currents meeting at right angles at a junction give a resultant of 4.24 A along the bisector.
With 6 C crossing the section in 3 s, the current is I = t/q = 0.5 A.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide when charge motion in a conductor becomes a net steady current rather than random motion or a temporary neutralisation current.
units.mechanism: A free charge in an electric field experiences a force and can contribute to current. In a solid conductor, current is carried by electrons; with no electric field their random thermal motion cancels, and a steady current requires a source in a closed circuit to keep charges supplied.

mx.cwo: The current in a copper wire is carried by positive metal ions drifting toward the negative terminal of the cell.
Connecting one end of a wire to a single terminal of a cell gives a steady current along it, because the field pushes the free electrons.
The current in the wire is what sets up the electric field inside it, so the field appears only after the electrons begin to move.
The current through copper sulphate solution is carried by free electrons moving through the liquid.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Classify whether a V-I relation is Ohmic instead of treating every use of V = IR as Ohm's law.
units.mechanism: Ohm's law is the proportionality V proportional to I for a conductor, so R is constant. The equation R = V/I defines resistance, while devices whose V-I relation changes with magnitude, sign, or uniqueness do not obey Ohm's law.

mx.cwo: The device whose V-I graph is a straight line cutting the voltage axis at 2 V is Ohmic, because the graph is a straight line.
A diode is Ohmic because its forward V-I graph is a straight line above 0.7 V.
A filament lamp is Ohmic, so its resistance stays at 10 ohm from 1 V right up to 240 V.
The GaAs sample is Ohmic because it is a solid piece of conducting material with two leads like any resistor.
The sample is Ohmic because R = rho l/A gives it one definite resistance from its length and area.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how changing a conductor's length, cross-sectional area, material, or temperature changes its resistance.
units.mechanism: For a uniform conductor, R = rho l/A. Increasing the length increases R in the same ratio; increasing the cross-sectional area decreases R in inverse ratio. Resistivity rho is a property of the material and depends on temperature, not on the conductor's dimensions.

mx.cwo: The resistivity of a 2 m length of copper wire is twice the resistivity of a 1 m length of the same wire.
For a wire tapering from 1 mm^2 to 0.25 mm^2 over 2 m, R = rho l/A with A = 0.625 mm^2, the average of the two areas.
Cutting the copper wire in half halves its resistivity as well as its resistance, from 1.7 x 10^-8 to 0.85 x 10^-8 ohm m.
For l = 2 m, A = 1 x 10^-6 m^2 and rho = 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm m, R = rho A/l = 8.5 x 10^-15 ohm.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Translate between current density, electric field, resistivity, and conductivity for an Ohmic conductor.
units.mechanism: Current density is j = I/A through an area normal to current. In a uniform Ohmic conductor, E l = j rho l, so E = j rho and j = sigma E with sigma = 1/rho; the vector current density is directed along E.

mx.cwo: The field along a wire carrying 2 A with rho = 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm m is E = I rho = 3.4 x 10^-8 V/m.
For a 2 m wire of radius 1 mm carrying 2 A, j = I/A with A the curved surface 1.26 x 10^-2 m^2, giving 159 A/m^2.
In the same electric field, nichrome with rho = 1.1 x 10^-6 ohm m carries a larger current density than copper.
In the tapering conductor the electric field is the same everywhere and equals j rho computed at the wide end.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Explain how electron drift and collisions produce Ohm's law microscopically.
units.mechanism: Without an electric field, electron velocities average to zero. With an electric field, electrons accelerate between collisions with acceleration -eE/m, and their average drift velocity is v_d = -(eE/m)tau. This gives j = (ne^2 tau/m)E and sigma = ne^2 tau/m when n and tau are independent of E.

mx.cwo: The electrons in the copper wire drift at about 10^5 m/s, the speed thermal motion gives them.
Ohm's law holds for every material, including a semiconductor whose carrier number rises as the applied field is raised.
The metal in which electrons collide more often is the better conductor, because the collisions pass the current along the wire.
Even with the field applied the average electron velocity is zero, because collisions randomise every direction equally.
Conductivity is sigma = n^2 e tau/m, so doubling the carrier density multiplies the conductivity by four.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how slow electron drift can coexist with nearly immediate establishment of current, and compute mobility from drift.
units.mechanism: Electron drift speed in a metal can be only a few millimetres per second, but closing a circuit establishes the electric field throughout the circuit almost instantly, causing local drift at every point. Mobility is mu = |v_d|/E = e tau/m and is positive.

mx.cwo: The electrons travel from the cell to the lamp at nearly the speed of light, which is why the lamp lights the instant the switch is closed.
The mobility of conduction electrons in copper is -4.4 x 10^-3 m^2/V s, negative because the drift is opposite to the field.
The drift speed of the electrons is about 1 mm/s in every wire, whatever the current or the thickness of the conductor.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Compare how resistivity depends on material class and temperature.
units.mechanism: Materials are classified by increasing resistivity as conductors, semiconductors, and insulators. Over a limited temperature range, rho_T = rho_0[1 + alpha(T - T_0)]. In metals, rising temperature decreases tau while n is nearly unchanged, so rho increases; in semiconductors and insulators, n increases enough that rho decreases.

mx.cwo: Heating a copper wire raises its resistivity because the number of free electrons in the metal falls.
Using rho_T = rho_0[1 + alpha(T - T_0)] with alpha = 3.9 x 10^-3 per K, the resistivity of platinum at 20 K comes out negative and is reported as the answer.
Heating a silicon sample raises its resistivity while heating a copper wire lowers it.
Graphite is an insulator because it is black and dull rather than shiny like a metal.
The resistance of the wire rises on heating because the wire expands and becomes longer.
With rho_0 = 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm m at 0 C and alpha = 3.9 x 10^-3 per K, the resistivity at 100 C is rho_0[1 + alpha x 373] = 4.2 x 10^-8 ohm m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Calculate electrical energy dissipation and choose the right power form for heating or transmission loss.
units.mechanism: When charge Delta Q = I Delta t moves through potential drop V, its potential energy decreases by IV Delta t and collisions dissipate that energy as heat. Power is P = IV, and for an Ohmic resistance P = I^2R = V^2/R. For transmission at fixed delivered power P through wire resistance R_c, wasted power is P_c = P^2 R_c/V^2.

mx.cwo: A 60 W lamp run for 2 hours uses 60 J of energy.
The diode carries 0.5 A at 0.7 V and an earlier reading gave 20 ohm, so it dissipates I^2R = 5 W.
Sending the same 100 kW at 220 kV instead of 22 kV multiplies the line loss by 100, because the higher voltage drives a bigger current through the cable.
The 5 ohm transmission line at 220 kV wastes V^2/R = 9.7 x 10^9 W.
With I = 2 A through R = 5 ohm, P = IR^2 = 50 W.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how a cell's emf, internal resistance, terminal voltage, and circuit current are related.
units.mechanism: A cell's emf epsilon is the open-circuit potential difference, not a force. With internal resistance r and load R during discharge, terminal voltage is V = epsilon - Ir = IR and the current is I = epsilon/(R + r). The maximum current for R = 0 is epsilon/r.

mx.cwo: The emf of the cell is 5.6 V, the voltmeter reading taken while it drives 2 A through the lamp.
With epsilon = 2 V, r = 1 ohm and R = 0.5 ohm, the current is I = epsilon/R = 4 A.
With epsilon = 6 V, r = 0.5 ohm and I = 2 A, the terminal voltage is V = epsilon + Ir = 7 V.
With epsilon = 6 V and r = 0.5 ohm the current through a 12 ohm lamp is 12 A, the largest the cell can supply.
The cell is marked 1.5 V, so the potential difference across the 2 ohm resistor it drives is 1.5 V.
With epsilon = 6 V, R = 10 ohm and r = 2 ohm, the current is I = 6/10 + 6/2 = 3.6 A.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Reduce cells in series or parallel to an equivalent emf and internal resistance with the correct signs.
units.mechanism: Cells in combination can be replaced by one equivalent cell. In series with the same assisting orientation, epsilon_eq = epsilon_1 + epsilon_2 and r_eq = r_1 + r_2; a reversed cell contributes negative emf. In parallel, 1/r_eq = sum_i 1/r_i and epsilon_eq/r_eq = sum_i epsilon_i/r_i.

mx.cwo: Two 2 V cells joined positive to negative in parallel still give an equivalent emf of 2 V.
A 6 V cell assisting a 2 V cell in series gives 4 V, while the same pair with one cell reversed gives 8 V.
The 2 V cell in the left branch and the 3 V cell in the right branch can be replaced by a single 5 V cell in series with the network.
Two 2 V cells in parallel give 1/epsilon_eq = 1/2 + 1/2, so epsilon_eq = 1 V.
With epsilon_1 = 2 V, r_1 = 1 ohm, epsilon_2 = 3 V and r_2 = 2 ohm, the equivalent emf is 2/1 + 3/2 = 3.5 V.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Set up Kirchhoff equations with consistent current directions and potential-change signs.
units.mechanism: For steady currents, at any junction the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving because charge does not accumulate. Around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of potential changes due to cells and resistors is zero because the path returns to the same potential. A negative solved current means the actual direction is opposite the chosen arrow.

mx.cwo: At the junction the algebraic sum of the potential changes is zero, so V_1 + V_2 + V_3 = 0 at that point.
While the capacitor charges, the current entering the plate must equal the current leaving it, so the current in that branch is zero.
Going round the loop in the direction of the 2 A current, the 5 ohm resistor contributes +10 V to the sum of potential changes.
The three-loop network gives three independent loop equations, so with two junction equations there are five equations for the three unknown currents.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Recognize when a Wheatstone bridge is balanced and use the balance condition instead of solving the full network.
units.mechanism: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, galvanometer current I_g = 0. Then I_1 = I_3 and I_2 = I_4, and Kirchhoff loop equations give R_2/R_1 = R_4/R_3, equivalently R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4. An unknown arm can then be found from the other three resistances.

mx.cwo: The bridge is balanced only when all four arms have the same resistance, so 10, 20, 15 and 30 ohm cannot be a balanced set.
In any two parallel branches the resistance ratios must be equal, so no current can flow in a link joining their midpoints.
The galvanometer shows only a small deflection, so the bridge is balanced and R_4 = R_2R_3/R_1 = 30 ohm.
The equivalent resistance of the bridge is always (R_1 + R_2) in parallel with (R_3 + R_4), because the galvanometer arm can be ignored.
With R_1 = 10 ohm, R_2 = 20 ohm and R_3 = 15 ohm, the ratio R_2/R_1 = R_3/R_4 gives R_4 = 7.5 ohm.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: When a diagram uses a dot or a cross, decide whether the current or field is directed out of the page or into the page.
units.mechanism: A dot denotes a current or field emerging out of the plane of the paper; a cross denotes a current or field going into the plane of the paper.

mx.cwo: The dot at the centre of the wire cross-section means the current is going into the page, away from the reader.
The circle with a dot in the figure marks a positive charge and the circle with a cross marks a negative charge.
The cross on the field region means the magnetic field there is zero, because a cross marks something cancelled out.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Given a charged particle's charge, velocity, and the electric and magnetic fields, decide the Lorentz-force direction and magnitude.
units.mechanism: The total force is F = q(E + v x B); the magnetic part q(v x B) is perpendicular to both v and B, vanishes when v is zero or parallel to B, and reverses direction when the charge sign reverses.

mx.cwo: A 2 C charge moving at 3 m/s across a 0.5 T field feels a magnetic force of qB = 1 N.
A proton moving at 10^6 m/s along the lines of a 0.2 T field feels a force of 3.2 x 10^-14 N.
For motion east in a field pointing north the positive charge is pushed downward and the electron upward.
In crossed fields the electric force qE acts at right angles to E, so the total force on the charge is perpendicular to both fields.
A negative charge is pulled toward the north pole of the magnet because unlike poles and unlike charges attract.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, decide the magnetic force from the current direction, length element, and external field.
units.mechanism: For a straight rod, F = I l x B, where l has the rod length and the direction of the current; for a wire of arbitrary shape, add the contributions I dl x B along the wire.

mx.cwo: The force on a 2 m rod carrying 5 A is F = IlB with B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r), the field of the rod itself.
A semicircular wire of arc length 1 m carrying 3 A in a 0.4 T field feels F = IlB = 1.2 N in the same direction as a straight wire would.
No force can be found for a wire lying at 30 degrees to the field, because F = IlB works only when the wire is at right angles to B.
The 50 cm wire crossing a 10 cm pole gap feels F = I x 0.5 x B, using the whole length of the wire.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field, decide whether the path is circular, helical, or undeflected and compute the orbit quantities.
units.mechanism: Because the magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity, a perpendicular velocity component undergoes circular motion with r = mv/(qB) and omega = qB/m; a parallel velocity component is unchanged, giving a helix with pitch p = 2*pi*m*v_parallel/(qB).

mx.cwo: The cyclotron frequency of a proton in a 0.5 T field is qB/m = 4.8 x 10^7 Hz.
A proton entering the field near a bar magnet moves in a circle of radius mv/(qB) using the field value at the entry point.
Doubling the proton's speed doubles its rotation frequency in the same magnetic field and leaves the radius unchanged.
A proton moving exactly along the field lines still travels in a circle of radius mv/(qB).
A proton entering a uniform magnetic field at right angles follows a parabola, curving more sharply the deeper it goes.
For v_parallel = 10^5 m/s and v_perpendicular = 2 x 10^5 m/s in a 0.1 T field, the pitch is 2 pi m v_perpendicular/(qB) = 0.13 m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a current element and a field point, decide the magnetic-field contribution using the Biot-Savart law.
units.mechanism: The field contribution of a current element is dB = (mu_0/4*pi) I(dl x r)/r^3, with magnitude |dB| = (mu_0 I dl sin theta)/(4*pi*r^2) and direction given by dl x r.

mx.cwo: With I = 10 A, dl = 1 mm, theta = 90 degrees and r = 0.02 m, dB = mu_0 I dl/(4 pi r) = 5 x 10^-8 T.
The current element pointing directly at P contributes dB = mu_0 I dl/(4 pi r^2), with sin theta taken as one.
The element pointing straight at P gives the largest field there, while the element at right angles to r gives none.
The field at the centre of a 5 cm circular loop carrying 2 A is mu_0 I l/(4 pi r^2) with l the whole circumference treated as one element.
For a current element along +x and a displacement along +y, dB at P points along -z because the direction is r cross dl.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a circular current loop, decide the magnetic field on its axis or at its centre by using symmetry and the loop right-hand rule.
units.mechanism: On the axis of a circular loop, B = mu_0 I R^2/[2(x^2 + R^2)^(3/2)] along the axis; at the centre this becomes B = mu_0 I/(2R), and N closely wound turns multiply the field by N.

mx.cwo: The field at the centre of a 0.1 m radius loop carrying 2 A is mu_0 I/(2 pi R) = 4 x 10^-6 T.
The field 5 cm to the side of the loop, off its axis, is mu_0 I R^2/[2(x^2 + R^2)^(3/2)] with x = 0.05 m.
With the current running clockwise as seen from the front, the field at the centre of the loop points out of the loop toward the viewer.
The field 10 cm along the axis from a 5 cm loop carrying 2 A is mu_0 I/(2R) = 2.5 x 10^-5 T, the same as at the centre.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide when Ampere's circuital law can simplify a magnetic-field calculation and how it gives the field of a long straight wire.
units.mechanism: Ampere's circuital law is integral B dot dl around a closed loop = mu_0 I_enclosed; with sufficient symmetry this reduces to BL = mu_0 I_enclosed, and for a long straight wire B = mu_0 I/(2*pi*r).

mx.cwo: The amperian loop encircles one of the two wires, but BL = mu_0(I_1 + I_2) because both currents appear in the diagram.
The field around a wire whose current is changing rapidly is still mu_0 I/(2 pi r) using the instantaneous conduction current, since the law always holds in that form.
The circular loop drawn beside the wire encloses no current, so B is zero at every point of that loop.
For a square amperian loop of side 10 cm around a wire carrying 4 A, B = mu_0 I/(4 x 0.1) = 1.3 x 10^-5 T at every point of the square.
Because the amperian loop is drawn as a circle, B is the same at every point on it and equals mu_0 I/(2 pi r), even though the wire is off centre.
For a 2 m wire carrying 5 A, B x 2 = mu_0 x 5, so B = 3.1 x 10^-6 T.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a solenoid, decide whether the long-solenoid approximation applies and compute the interior magnetic field.
units.mechanism: For a long solenoid with n turns per unit length carrying current I, the interior field is B = mu_0 n I; in the ideal long-solenoid picture, the exterior field approaches zero.

mx.cwo: For n = 1000 turns per metre and I = 2 A, the interior field is (mu_0/4 pi) n I = 2 x 10^-4 T.
A 4 cm long coil of radius 3 cm with 200 turns carrying 1 A has B = mu_0 n I = 6.3 x 10^-3 T inside and exactly zero outside.
Stretching a 500-turn solenoid from 25 cm to 50 cm at the same current doubles the field inside it.
For 500 turns of radius 2 cm carrying 1 A, the field inside the coil is N mu_0 I/(2R) = 1.6 x 10^-2 T.
For 500 turns over 0.25 m, n = 0.25/500 = 5 x 10^-4 per metre and B = mu_0 n I = 6.3 x 10^-10 T.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For two long parallel current-carrying conductors, decide whether the force is attractive or repulsive and compute the force per unit length.
units.mechanism: The field of one long wire at the other is B = mu_0 I/(2*pi*d), so the force per unit length is f = mu_0 I_a I_b/(2*pi*d); currents in the same direction attract and currents in opposite directions repel.

mx.cwo: Two 3 m wires 1 m apart each carrying 5 A attract with a force of 5 x 10^-6 N.
Two 5 cm wires crossing at right angles 2 mm apart attract with f = mu_0 I_a I_b/(2 pi d).
The 1 m spacing and 1 A definition can be checked with two ordinary wires on the bench, since stray fields make no difference to the force between them.
The two wires whose arrows are drawn pointing toward each other attract, and the pair drawn pointing apart repel.
Two wires 0.5 m apart carrying 4 A and 6 A have f = mu_0 I_a I_b/(2 pi d^2) = 1.9 x 10^-5 N/m.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a current loop in a uniform magnetic field, decide the torque, magnetic moment, and equilibrium orientation.
units.mechanism: A current loop in a uniform magnetic field has zero net force but can have torque tau = m x B, with m = N I A in the area-vector direction; the torque magnitude is N I A B sin theta and vanishes when m is parallel or antiparallel to B.

mx.cwo: For a 50-turn square coil of side 4 cm carrying 2 A, m = N I A with A the perimeter 0.16 m, giving m = 16 A m.
A current loop held near one pole of a bar magnet has zero net force on it, because a loop in a magnetic field only experiences a torque.
The torque on the coil is largest when its magnetic moment points along the field and zero when the moment is at right angles to the field.
With the plane of the coil at 30 degrees to the field, the torque is N I A B sin 30 = 0.5 N I A B.
Each of the four arms of the square coil feels IlB the same way, so the coil is pushed sideways with a total force of 4IlB.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide when a planar current loop may be treated as a magnetic dipole and what far-field form follows.
units.mechanism: At large distances, a planar current loop behaves like a magnetic dipole with magnetic moment m = I A; for a circular loop on its axis and x much larger than R, B = mu_0 I A/(2*pi*x^3), and the corresponding far field in the loop plane is proportional to (mu_0/4*pi)m/x^3.

mx.cwo: For a loop of radius 4 cm carrying 3 A, the magnetic moment is m = IR = 0.12 A m.
Doubling the axial distance from the loop halves the far field rather than reducing it to one eighth.
At 30 cm in the plane of the loop, B = mu_0 2m/(4 pi x^3), the same expression as on the axis.
The far field of the loop in its plane falls as one over x squared, following the electric dipole result.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: For a moving-coil galvanometer, decide how current produces pointer deflection.
units.mechanism: In the galvanometer's radial magnetic field, the magnetic torque on the N-turn coil is tau = N I A B; the spring torque balances it as k phi = N I A B, so phi = (NAB/k) I.

mx.cwo: As the coil turns to 60 degrees the magnetic torque falls to N I A B sin 60, so the deflection is not proportional to the current.
The pointer swings first and its motion drives a current round the coil, which is what the meter registers.
A 30 division deflection means 5 mA on any galvanometer, since deflection is proportional to current.
The galvanometer with the longer pointer is more sensitive because its tip moves further for the same current.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to convert a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter and how that affects sensitivity.
units.mechanism: A galvanometer becomes an ammeter by adding a very small shunt resistance in parallel, giving effective resistance about r_s; it becomes a voltmeter by adding a large resistance in series, and voltage sensitivity is phi/V = (NAB/k)(1/R).

mx.cwo: Increasing the number of turns N raises the voltage sensitivity phi/V in the same proportion as it raises phi/I.
An ammeter of resistance 50 ohm placed in series with a 10 ohm resistor still reads the current that flowed before it was inserted.
A galvanometer becomes an ammeter by adding a large resistance in series and a voltmeter by adding a small shunt in parallel.
The instrument marked A can be connected across the lamp, because an ammeter measures current wherever it is placed.
To convert a 100 ohm, 1 mA galvanometer into a 1 A ammeter, r_s = R_G(I - I_g)/I_g = 9.99 x 10^4 ohm.

units.subject: physics
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a magnetic field-line drawing correctly shows the direction, strength, and non-force meaning of the magnetic field.
units.mechanism: The tangent to a magnetic field line gives the direction of the net magnetic field at that point, closer line spacing means a stronger field, and magnetic field lines show compass-needle alignment rather than the force direction on a moving charge.
